title: bug(cli): ao doctor gitlab-token probe hardcodes gitlab.com, ignores self-managed host config
body:
## Bug

`ao doctor`'s `gitlab-token` check always probes `https://gitlab.com/api/v4/user`, regardless of `AO_GITLAB_ALLOWED_HOSTS` / `AO_GITLAB_HOST_TOKENS`. On a self-managed GitLab install the check reports a token verdict about a host AO will never call: a valid self-hosted PAT reads as `FAIL ... token rejected by GitLab (HTTP 401)`, and a broken self-hosted setup can read as `PASS`.

**Reported by:** @MCMXC | **Analyzed against:** `bc68557ff`
**Confidence:** High

## Reproduction

1. `export AO_GITLAB_ALLOWED_HOSTS=gitlab.example.com`
2. `export AO_GITLAB_TOKEN=<PAT valid on gitlab.example.com>`
3. `ao doctor`
4. GitLab section reports on gitlab.com; the probe URL in the failure is `gitlab.com/api/v4/user`. `gitlab.example.com` is never contacted.

## Root Cause

`backend/internal/cli/doctor.go`:

- `defaultDoctorGitLabRESTBase = "https://gitlab.com/api/v4"` (line 56) is the only base the check knows.
- `checkGitLabToken` builds the probe from `c.deps.DoctorGitLabRESTBase` unconditionally (line ~519) and never consults `cfg.GitLab`.
- `runDoctor` loads `config.Load()` (which populates `cfg.GitLab.AllowedHosts` / `cfg.GitLab.HostTokens` from `AO_GITLAB_ALLOWED_HOSTS` / `AO_GITLAB_HOST_TOKENS`) but does not pass it to the GitLab check.
- Token selection has the same gap: the per-host override in `AO_GITLAB_HOST_TOKENS` is ignored; the check always uses the default `AO_GITLAB_TOKEN`/`GITLAB_TOKEN`/`glab` token.

The SCM provider already does this correctly — `Provider.clientForHost` (`backend/internal/adapters/scm/gitlab/provider.go`) derives `https://<host>/api/v4` per allowlisted host and selects the per-host token. Doctor is the one code path that never got host awareness.

Note: there is no `AO_GITLAB_HOST` variable and no `scmConfig.host` YAML key in the Go backend — host config is `AO_GITLAB_ALLOWED_HOSTS` (+ `AO_GITLAB_HOST_TOKENS`) only.

## Fix

Make the check host-aware, mirroring `clientForHost`:

- No allowlist configured → probe the default instance as today (check name `gitlab-token`).
- Allowlist configured → one check per host, named `gitlab-token:<host>`, probing `https://<host>/api/v4/user` (port preserved), with the `AO_GITLAB_HOST_TOKENS` override when present and the default token otherwise. `gitlab.com`/`www.gitlab.com` in the allowlist keep the default base.

## Impact

- Self-managed GitLab users get a false `FAIL` on a working token and no signal at all about the host they actually use.
- Doctor sends the token to gitlab.com for deployments that intentionally never talk to gitlab.com.
- Per-host tokens are never validated.

title: feat(gitlab): support self-managed instances on http or under a path prefix
body:
## Problem

The GitLab SCM provider derives a self-managed REST base as `https://<host>/api/v4` and nothing else is reachable:

- `backend/internal/adapters/scm/gitlab/provider.go` (`clientForHost`) hardcodes the `https://` scheme — a deliberate "reject HTTPS-to-HTTP downgrades" decision, documented in the function comment.
- The path is always `/api/v4`, so an instance served under a prefix (`https://git.example.com/gitlab`) cannot be addressed.
- `backend/internal/cli/doctor.go` mirrors both constraints via `DoctorGitLabHostRESTBase`.

Both shapes are common in on-prem deployments: a plain-HTTP instance behind a VPN or an internal TLS-terminating proxy, and a GitLab mounted under a path on a shared hostname.

## Impact

Such a deployment cannot be used with AO at all. `AO_GITLAB_ALLOWED_HOSTS` accepts the host, the derived base is wrong, and every SCM and tracker call fails with a transport or 404 error that does not name the cause.

## Possible direction

Accept a full base URL in the allowlist entry (e.g. `AO_GITLAB_ALLOWED_HOSTS="http://gitlab.internal:8080,https://git.example.com/gitlab"`), keeping bare hosts meaning `https://<host>/api/v4`. Plain HTTP should stay opt-in and explicit, since it sends the token in clear text; the allowlist is already the trust boundary that makes that an operator decision rather than a silent downgrade.

Documented as unsupported in `frontend/src/landing/content/docs/plugins/scm/gitlab.mdx`.

## Related

- [#4206](https://github.com/Untrivial-ai/agent-orchestrator/issues/4206) — doctor's gitlab-token probe hardcoded gitlab.com

title: feat(gitlab): allow a custom CA bundle for self-managed instances
body:
## Problem

The GitLab client uses a default `http.Client` with no TLS configuration (`backend/internal/adapters/scm/gitlab/client.go`, `NewClient`), so certificate verification relies entirely on the operating system trust store. `ao doctor`'s probe uses the CLI's shared client and has the same property.

Self-managed GitLab installs commonly terminate TLS with a certificate from a private/corporate CA. If that CA is not installed system-wide, every SCM and tracker call fails with an x509 verification error, and the operator's only remedies are outside AO (install the CA into the OS store, or terminate TLS elsewhere).

## Impact

- No AO-level way to trust an internal CA; the failure surfaces as a transport error rather than a configuration message.
- On machines where the user cannot modify the system trust store, GitLab support is unusable.

## Possible direction

An `AO_GITLAB_CA_CERT` (path to a PEM bundle) that seeds a `tls.Config.RootCAs` for the GitLab clients — additive to the system pool, per-provider, and never a verification-disabling switch. `InsecureSkipVerify` should stay unavailable: the allowlist plus a token makes a silent MITM opt-out too costly.

Documented as a limitation in `frontend/src/landing/content/docs/plugins/scm/gitlab.mdx`.

## Related

- [#4207](https://github.com/Untrivial-ai/agent-orchestrator/issues/4207) — self-managed instances on http or under a path prefix

title: fix(gitlab): make doctor and daemon credentials host-aware
body:
Code changes: +888 -119
Tests: +1316 -4
Others: +73 -2

## What

Makes GitLab credential handling host-aware in both `ao doctor` and the daemon, so self-managed instances are actually supported end to end.

- `ao doctor` now emits one check per configured instance: `gitlab-token` for gitlab.com and `gitlab-token:<host>` for every `AO_GITLAB_ALLOWED_HOSTS` entry, resolving the `AO_GITLAB_HOST_TOKENS` override exactly the way the SCM provider does.
- The daemon's gitlab.com token chain scopes its `glab` lookup to gitlab.com, and never consults `glab`'s own default host unscoped.
- Each allowlisted host without an explicit override gets a chain that asks `glab` about that host specifically (`--hostname`), shared by the SCM provider and the tracker.
- `glab` output is attributed to hosts by parsing, not by exit code, and only a line that actually names a credential is read as one.
- `GLabTokenSource` memoizes failures for 30s.
- The GitLab tracker no longer refuses to construct when the only credentials are per-host ones.
- Docs: new GitLab SCM and GitLab tracker pages, self-managed host configuration, and the doctor attribution rules.

## Why

Before this, `ao doctor` only ever probed gitlab.com. A self-managed deployment never reaches gitlab.com, so the one GitLab check reported a verdict about a host AO would never call — and it did so by sending whatever token it found to gitlab.com, which could be the internal instance's PAT.

Credential attribution is the core rule the change introduces: **a token is only ever sent to the instance it can be attributed to.** Sending an internal token to gitlab.com discloses it to a third party; sending gitlab.com's token to a self-managed instance hands it to whoever runs that server. All tokens are resolved before any request is issued, and a probe whose credential cannot be attributed to its own host is reported as skipped, with the reason and the fix (`glab auth login --hostname <host>`, or an `AO_GITLAB_HOST_TOKENS` entry).

The daemon changes close the gap the doctor work exposed. An unscoped `glab auth status --show-token` prints every configured host and the first token line wins, which is not necessarily the host being asked about — so a multi-instance `glab` setup could send an internal PAT to gitlab.com while doctor, scoping its own lookup correctly, reported the gitlab.com token as valid.

## How

Reviewer-relevant decisions:

- **Attribution.** A credential counts as attributed to a host when it comes from that host's `AO_GITLAB_HOST_TOKENS` entry, from `glab auth status --hostname <host>`, or from a `glab` status block that names the host as the token's owner. `AO_GITLAB_TOKEN`/`GITLAB_TOKEN` are a global default: the daemon offers them to every instance, but nothing attributes them to any particular one.
- **Doctor is stricter than the daemon, in both directions.** It probes an instance only with a credential attributable to that instance, so two cases are reported instead of probed: a self-managed host reached solely by the global default (that value is most likely gitlab.com's, and probing would hand it to whoever operates the internal server, then report the inevitable 401 as a credential failure), and gitlab.com when an allowlisted host binds that same value (nothing can say which instance it belongs to). Both messages name the remedy. The daemon still offers the global default everywhere at runtime — that is the documented meaning of a global default — doctor just declines to validate it where it cannot attribute it.
- **gitlab.com is strict unconditionally.** Its chain is env vars, then `glab` scoped to gitlab.com; there is no unscoped fallback in the chain itself, whatever the allowlist says. A `glab` too old for `--hostname` still works, because the lookup falls back to the unscoped status block and accepts only the token that block attributes to gitlab.com.
- **Exit codes do not gate parsing.** `glab auth status` exits non-zero when *any* configured instance is unauthenticated, while still printing a usable block for the ones that are — one stale session must not strand every other host. What keeps a diagnostic from being read as a credential is the parsing: only `Token:` / `Token found:` lines name the credential (so `Token expires: <date>` is rejected), and a value containing whitespace is rejected outright, because no GitLab token contains a space and `error: Token: expired or revoked` is prose.
- **`--hostname` is a request, not a guarantee.** A `glab` that ignores it prints the full multi-instance block, where the first token line belongs to whichever host it listed first. Scoped output is therefore read host-attributed first, and the unattributed first-token reading is used only when the output names no instance at all.
- **Unreachable ≠ invalid.** A transport failure against a self-managed host (VPN down, split DNS) is a warning, not a failure; it says nothing about the credential. A 401/403 is still a hard failure, because a probe only ever runs against an instance whose credential could be attributed to it.
- **Empty `host=` entries** in `AO_GITLAB_HOST_TOKENS` are treated as "no override" in both doctor and the daemon — binding `StaticTokenSource("")` would give the host a source that can only ever fail, silently disabling it — and the `gitlab-host-tokens` check reports them, alongside entries whose host is not allowlisted and entries for gitlab.com. An entry the user believes is in use that nothing reads is exactly the misconfiguration that check exists to surface.
- **Failure memoization.** A host-scoped source `glab` cannot satisfy fails on every call, forking a process per token resolution (once per allowlisted host, on every API call and every doctor probe). Failures are memoized for 30s — far shorter than the 5m success TTL, so a fresh `glab auth login` becomes visible quickly — and `InvalidateToken` clears the memo. A failure caused by the caller's own context cancellation is never memoized: startup probes several hosts under one deadline and cancels the losers, and caching those would answer the next caller with a live context out of a stale failure.
- **Doctor probes hosts concurrently.** Each host costs a `glab` lookup plus an HTTPS probe, both bounded by `probeTimeout`; serially, four off-VPN hosts is ~18s of wall clock in a command users expect to be quick. Credential resolution and probes now run in parallel, so doctor waits for the slowest host rather than the sum. The `glab` memo is mutex-guarded; the lock is never held across the subprocess, so two goroutines may race to run the same key, which is harmless for a command that only reads local credential state.
- **Tracker construction.** `trackergitlab.New` still fails fast, but "no token" now means *no instance* can authenticate. A self-managed-only setup keeps its credential in `AO_GITLAB_HOST_TOKENS` and has nothing for gitlab.com; disabling the tracker there left issue intake dead for the only instance the user talks to. gitlab.com lookups now fail per request instead. The constructor's existence probe runs the allowlisted hosts concurrently under a single deadline — serially, three slow hosts on the daemon's synchronous startup path could stall boot ~15s past the default source's own budget — and the first host that answers cancels the rest, since one usable instance is all the check needs.

Intentional omissions: self-managed API traffic is always `https://<host>/api/v4` — plain HTTP and path-prefixed instances (`https://host/gitlab`) are not supported, and a private CA must be trusted by the OS (AO has no separate CA setting). This matches the provider's existing `clientForHost` behavior and is documented on the GitLab SCM page.

## Testing

- `go build ./...`, `go vet ./internal/...`, `gofmt -l internal/` — clean.
- `go test ./...` — 5976 passed.
- `go test -race` on the GitLab SCM, GitLab tracker, CLI, and daemon packages — clean, including the new concurrent doctor probes.
- New coverage: multi-instance doctor probes, per-host token selection and case-insensitive host matching, empty `host=` overrides (ignored as credentials, reported as misconfiguration), unreachable self-managed hosts, `glab` command-failure diagnostics, both directions of the credential boundary (an internal token never sent to gitlab.com, the global default never sent to a self-managed host), a usable host block read out of a non-zero `glab` run, `Token expires:` never mistaken for a credential, host-scoped token chains in the daemon wiring, `GLabTokenSource` failure memoization and recovery, and tracker construction with per-host credentials only.
- `npx prettier --check` on the touched MDX pages — clean.

## Checklist

- [x] Branched from `main` (or continuing an existing PR branch)
- [x] One focused change; links the related issue when applicable
- [x] Follows [AGENTS.md](https://github.com/AgentWrapper/agent-orchestrator/blob/main/AGENTS.md) conventions and PR hygiene
- [x] Tests added/updated for user-visible behavior where it makes sense
- [x] Relevant CI checks pass for the area touched (`go`, frontend, etc.)

title: bug(cli): transient daemon restart is reported to agents as a hook error on stderr
body:
## Summary

Every hook that fires while the daemon is restarting prints `AO daemon is not running (stale run-file at ...) — start it with \`ao start\`` onto stderr. Hooks run inside the agent's own process, so that text lands in the agent's context as if the tool had failed.

The hook itself is fine — it exits 0, and reconciliation recovers the missed activity from process state. The problem is purely that an expected, transient condition is reported to the agent as an error.

## Why it happens

The desktop app's daemon takeover removes the old run-file and the new daemon writes a fresh one (`frontend/src/main.ts:1261`). Between those two steps the run-file still holds the **previous daemon's dead PID**.

Any CLI call in that window hits `backend/internal/cli/client.go:129`:

```go
if !c.deps.ProcessAlive(info.PID) {
    return fmt.Errorf("AO daemon is not running (stale run-file at %s) — start it with `ao start`", cfg.RunFilePath)
}
```

The error is an untyped `fmt.Errorf`, so `reportHookFailure` (`backend/internal/cli/hooks.go:450`) cannot distinguish "the daemon is mid-restart" from "the daemon returned 500", and unconditionally writes it to `c.deps.Err`.

The same applies to the `info == nil` branch just above it (no run-file at all).

## Observed impact

From one machine's `$AO_DATA_DIR/hooks.log`, **56 occurrences across 9 distinct restart windows** since late June. All hook events are affected:

| hook | count |
|---|---|
| `claude-code session-end` | 27 |
| `agent-process process-exited` | 7 |
| `claude-code user-prompt-submit` | 4 |
| `claude-code session-start` | 3 |
| `claude-code pre-tool-use` | 3 |
| `claude-code post-tool-use` | 3 |
| `claude-code stop` | 3 |
| `claude-code notification` | 3 |
| `opencode user-prompt-submit` | 2 |
| `opencode session-start` | 1 |

One representative window lasted ~35 seconds and hit 6 concurrent sessions across 5 projects. Where agent transcripts recorded the invocation (12 of them), every one shows `"exitCode": 0` — confirming the hooks worked and only the message was spurious. `agent-process process-exited` fires after the agent is gone, so it appears in `hooks.log` only, which does not record an exit code.

Session-start context injection is unaffected: it is read from disk and emitted before any daemon call (`hooks.go:311`), so it still reaches the agent during a restart window.

Both agent adapters that use hooks are affected, so this is not `claude-code`-specific.

## Impact

- Agents receive a spurious "daemon is not running" error in their context and may act on it — re-running work, reporting failure, or asking the user to run `ao start` when the daemon is in fact healthy.
- The message is indistinguishable from a genuine daemon outage, so real problems are harder to spot in `hooks.log`.

## Reproduction

No live daemon required — `ProcessAlive` is already injectable via `Deps` (`backend/internal/cli/root.go:70`):

```go
func TestHooks_DaemonNotRunningStaysOutOfStderr(t *testing.T) {
	t.Setenv("AO_SESSION_ID", "ao-7")
	cfg := setConfigEnv(t)
	if err := runfile.Write(cfg.runFile, runfile.Info{
		PID: 999999, Port: 3001, StartedAt: time.Unix(100, 0).UTC(),
	}); err != nil {
		t.Fatalf("write run-file: %v", err)
	}

	_, errOut, err := executeCLI(t, Deps{
		In:           strings.NewReader(`{"reason":"logout"}`),
		ProcessAlive: func(int) bool { return false },
	}, "hooks", "claude-code", "session-end")
	if err != nil {
		t.Fatalf("hooks must exit 0 when the daemon is down, got: %v", err)
	}
	if errOut != "" {
		t.Errorf("daemon-down must not reach the agent's stderr, got %q", errOut)
	}
}
```

Currently fails with the stale-run-file message on stderr. The `info == nil` variant (no run-file, `ProcessAlive` returning true) reproduces the second branch.

## Suggested fix

Make the condition a sentinel so callers can classify it:

```go
var ErrDaemonNotRunning = errors.New("AO daemon is not running")
```

wrap it with `%w` in both branches of `doJSONPathWithHeadersAndTimeout`, and in `reportHookFailure` skip the stderr write when `errors.Is(cause, ErrDaemonNotRunning)` — still appending to `hooks.log` so the event stays diagnosable. Genuine daemon errors keep reaching stderr unchanged, and interactive commands keep the identical message text.

Happy to raise a PR (branch ready, red test → fix → green, mutation-checked).

title: fix(cli): keep daemon-down out of hook stderr
body:
Closes #4210.

Hooks run inside the agent's own process, so anything they write to stderr lands in the agent's context. During the desktop app's daemon takeover the run-file briefly points at a dead PID, and every hook firing in that window printed `AO daemon is not running (stale run-file at ...)` at the agent — even though the hook exits 0 and reconciliation recovers the missed activity from process state.

## Change

`doJSONPathWithHeadersAndTimeout` returned an untyped `fmt.Errorf` for both daemon-down branches, so `reportHookFailure` could not tell a restart apart from a real delivery failure.

- Add `ErrDaemonNotRunning` and wrap it with `%w` in both branches (`info == nil`, dead PID). Message text is unchanged, so interactive commands read exactly as before.
- In `reportHookFailure`, skip the stderr write when `errors.Is(cause, ErrDaemonNotRunning)`. The notice still goes to `hooks.log`, so the event stays diagnosable.

Genuine daemon errors (HTTP 5xx, transport failures) keep reaching stderr — covered by the existing `TestHooks_DaemonErrorIsSwallowed`, which is untouched and still asserts stderr is written.

## Tests

`TestHooks_DaemonNotRunningStaysOutOfStderr` is table-driven over both branches and needs no live daemon — `ProcessAlive` is injectable via `Deps`. It asserts exit 0, empty stderr, and a recorded `hooks.log` line.

Verified red before the fix (both sub-cases), green after. Mutation-checked: removing the `errors.Is` guard fails the test.

`go test ./internal/cli/` passes; `gofmt -l .` and `go vet ./...` are clean across the module.

title: bug(chat): transient Codex network loss is misreported as a fatal thread error
body:
## Bug

When a Codex Chat turn exhausts its reconnect attempts during a transient network outage, Codex app-server briefly reports the thread as `systemError`. AO persists that status and the desktop renders a banner claiming the provider thread is broken and future turns will usually fail. The prognosis is false: once connectivity returns, the next message succeeds on the same thread.

**Source:** AO chat report with read-only evidence from session `agent-orchestrator-140` | **Observed:** 2026-08-20 PDT | **Analyzed against:** `52fde0279` | **AO version:** locally built `dev`, daemon on port 3001
**Confidence:** High
**Priority:** P2 — Chat is degraded and the banner discourages the working recovery path, but sending a new message after connectivity returns is a workaround.

## Reproduction

1. Start a Codex session in Chat mode and begin a turn.
2. Disconnect the machine from the network long enough for Codex to exhaust its response-stream reconnect attempts.
3. Observe Codex app-server emit `thread/status/changed` with `status.type = systemError`, followed by `turn/completed` with a failed turn and a transport error such as `stream disconnected before completion: error sending request for url (https://chatgpt.com/backend-api/codex/responses)`.
4. Observe AO render “The agent's thread hit an internal error” and say new turns will usually fail.
5. Restore connectivity and send another message. The same thread becomes `active`, answers normally, and returns to `idle`.

Concrete incident timeline (2026-08-20 PDT):

- 14:57:26 — turn `01a0212d-d469-75c1-b54b-4707757194be` became active.
- 15:03:44 — laptop entered clamshell sleep and Wi-Fi dropped; Codex emitted two five-attempt reconnect cycles, including macOS DNS lookup failure and an error sending the responses request.
- 15:24:33 — provider emitted `systemError`, then completed the turn as failed with the transport error.
- 16:59:43 — next user turn `01a0219d-c59c-73c2-8921-d12975cef2b9` became active on the same provider conversation.
- 17:07:55 — that turn completed normally and the thread returned to idle.

## Root Cause

- `backend/internal/adapters/chatdriver/codexappserver/normalize.go` maps every Codex `systemError` thread status directly to `domain.ThreadStatusSystemError` without correlating it with the immediately following failed turn.
- The same normalizer preserves the `turn/completed` error text but does not classify transport signatures or repair the pessimistic thread state.
- `backend/internal/service/chat/controller.go` persists thread-state updates independently. Therefore the transient `system_error` is sticky until a later provider status report replaces it.
- `frontend/src/renderer/components/chat/ChatStatusBanners.tsx` treats every `system_error` as a durable provider-thread fault and explicitly predicts that new turns will usually fail.

Read-only durable evidence from the incident shows this exact event order:

1. `thread.state = active`
2. `thread.state = system_error`
3. `turn.completed = failed`, error `stream disconnected before completion: error sending request for url (...)`
4. on the next message, `thread.state = active`
5. `thread.state = idle`
6. `turn.completed = completed`

This falsifies the theory that AO derives `system_error` from any failed turn: Codex reports it. AO's bug is interpreting and persisting that provider status without the transport-failure context it reports milliseconds later.

## Fix

- Classify known transient Codex transport failures from the failed turn's error signature.
- Preserve the turn as failed and preserve its error text.
- Correlate the transport failure with the preceding `systemError`, restore the thread to a healthy idle state, and retain a current “connection lost during this turn” notice until the next turn begins.
- Render recovery-oriented copy that tells the user to send a message again.
- Keep genuine unclassified `systemError` behavior unchanged.
- Add adapter/service and renderer tests for transient versus genuine system errors and for clearing the connection-loss notice on the next active status.

## Impact

- Users are told a healthy, reusable conversation is probably permanently broken.
- The incorrect state remains visible throughout an outage and after connectivity returns, until another turn is attempted.
- Users may abandon context or restart work unnecessarily.

## Related

- [#4120](https://github.com/Untrivial-ai/agent-orchestrator/issues/4120) — also involved a failed Chat turn, but concerned TUI→Chat history settlement rather than transient thread-state classification.

title: feat(chat): retry a failed turn without retyping the prompt
body:
## Problem

When a Chat turn fails after transient network loss, AO preserves the failed turn and its error correctly, but the user has no one-click way to submit the same prompt again. They must retype or manually copy the original message.

This is especially confusing when the recovery guidance says to send the message again.

**Source:** Follow-up from [#4212](https://github.com/Untrivial-ai/agent-orchestrator/issues/4212) | **Analyzed against:** `52fde0279`
**Confidence:** High
**Priority:** P2 — the core recovery path works, but avoidable re-entry friction follows a common transient failure.

## Current Behavior

- A failed turn is durable and its original human message remains in the timeline.
- The turn boundary displays `Failed` and the provider error.
- Rollback and edit/branch operations exist, but no operation means “dispatch this failed human prompt again as a new turn.”
- The composer retains attachments only when the initial send itself fails before acceptance; it does not restore content for an asynchronously failed provider turn.

## Proposed Behavior

Add a **Retry turn** action to eligible failed-turn boundaries that:

1. Reuses the durable original human message content and attachments.
2. Creates a new turn rather than mutating or relabeling the failed attempt.
3. Preserves both attempts in history and keeps provider-turn correlation explicit.
4. Uses the conversation's current next-turn settings unless product design deliberately chooses to preserve the failed attempt's settings.
5. Is disabled while another turn is running and reports daemon/provider refusals in place.
6. Is safe against double-clicks and uncertain delivery; it must not silently execute the work twice.

## Scope Notes

This should be a dedicated daemon/API operation, not renderer-side reconstruction of message text. The daemon owns ordering, attachments, delivery state, and idempotency. Reusing the existing edit/fork path would change conversation history semantics and is not equivalent to retrying after a recoverable failure.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Retry is offered only for an eligible failed human turn.
- Clicking once creates exactly one new queued/running turn with the same content.
- The original failed turn remains failed and visible.
- Attachments are reused or a clear validation error explains why they cannot be.
- Busy, unsupported-provider, stale-branch, and uncertain-delivery cases are tested.
- Renderer tests cover visible, hidden, disabled, pending, and error states.

## Related

- [#4212](https://github.com/Untrivial-ai/agent-orchestrator/issues/4212) — classifies transient Codex network failures and provides accurate recovery guidance.

title: fix(chat): classify transient Codex transport failures
body:
Fixes [#4212](https://github.com/Untrivial-ai/agent-orchestrator/issues/4212).

## Summary

- classify narrow Codex response-stream transport signatures after the provider reports `systemError`
- preserve the failed turn and exact provider error while restoring the reusable thread to healthy `idle`
- retain a recoverable connection-loss notice until the next turn becomes active
- render accurate recovery guidance instead of predicting that future turns will fail
- leave genuine/unclassified provider `systemError` behavior unchanged
- regenerate OpenAPI and renderer API types for the optional connection-loss timestamp

## Evidence

In session `agent-orchestrator-140`, Codex emitted `thread/status/changed = systemError` immediately before a failed `turn/completed` with `stream disconnected before completion: error sending request for url (...)`. The same provider conversation accepted the next turn, became active, completed normally, and returned to idle. The durable AO event order confirms the status came from Codex; AO's fault was retaining and presenting it without the transport context reported milliseconds later.

## Tests

- `cd backend && go build ./...`
- `env -u AO_SESSION_ID -u AO_PROJECT_ID -u AO_DAEMON_URL -u AO_RUN_FILE -u AO_DATA_DIR -u AO_PORT npm run lint`
- `env -u AO_SESSION_ID -u AO_PROJECT_ID -u AO_DAEMON_URL -u AO_RUN_FILE -u AO_DATA_DIR -u AO_PORT sh -c 'cd backend && go test -race ./...'`
- `npm run api`
- `npm run frontend:typecheck`
- `cd frontend && npm test` — 2,630 passed, 1 skipped

## Risk / follow-up

Classification is intentionally limited to response-stream failures with known DNS/send/reset/closed/timeout transport signatures. Unknown errors continue to display the provider's genuine `systemError` state.

A one-click retry action is intentionally separate because it needs a daemon-owned, idempotent history/dispatch operation: [#4215](https://github.com/Untrivial-ai/agent-orchestrator/issues/4215).

title: feat: add provider-neutral subscription usage
body:
## Summary

Adds a provider-neutral subscription usage system for Codex, Claude, and future coding-agent adapters. The feature tracks provider-reported plan capacity, current rate-limit windows, credits/balances when available, bounded usage history, refresh failures, and threshold alerts without estimating prompts or tasks from token totals.

## Implementation

### Provider adapter layer

- Introduces a neutral quota model in `backend/internal/domain/quota.go` for provider accounts, limits, balances, capabilities, history points, and alerts.
- Adds quota ports so adapters can publish snapshots without the service depending on provider-specific payloads.
- Maps Codex app-server `account/rateLimits/read` and rate-limit update payloads into neutral quota snapshots, including:
  - account-level rate limits
  - model-scoped limits from `rateLimitsByLimitId`
  - Codex credits from `rateLimits.credits`
  - reset credits from `rateLimitResetCredits.availableCount`
  - duplicate-window collapse when Codex reports identical primary/secondary windows
- Maps Claude ACP usage metadata and structured plan usage into neutral quota snapshots, including:
  - partial push-based usage updates from ACP metadata
  - full sessionless reads through `ao-claude-plan-usage.mjs`
  - five-hour, seven-day, OAuth app, Opus, Sonnet, and model-scoped windows when Claude reports them
- Keeps provider-specific parsing inside the relevant adapter packages so future adapters can add quota support by implementing the same neutral contracts.

### Quota service

- Adds `backend/internal/service/quota` to merge provider observations, coalesce refreshes, cache fresh reads, derive severity, and emit transition-only alerts.
- Supports complete and partial snapshots so provider pushes do not erase previously known buckets.
- Refreshes per provider account rather than per session, which avoids multiplying provider calls when multiple conversations share one subscription.
- Registers daemon-owned providers and refreshes stale accounts on startup, periodically, on Plan Usage page entry, and after relevant idle transitions.
- Persists a first refresh failure for registered provider accounts so installed-but-broken providers appear as actionable error cards instead of disappearing from the page.

### Storage

- Adds SQLite migration `0102_provider_quota.sql` with:
  - `quota_accounts` for latest provider/account state
  - `quota_limits` for latest limit buckets
  - `quota_balances` for latest credits/balances
  - `quota_history` for bounded trend data
  - `quota_alerts` for threshold transitions
- Inserts history only when the meaningful quota state changes.
- Compacts history automatically:
  - last 24 hours: at most one point per minute
  - 24 hours to 30 days: at most one point per hour
  - 30 to 90 days: at most one point per day
  - older than 90 days: deleted

### API and frontend

- Adds daemon API endpoints for:
  - listing provider quota snapshots
  - fetching one provider account
  - refreshing one provider account
  - reading bounded history
  - reading recent quota alerts
- Regenerates OpenAPI and frontend TypeScript schema.
- Adds a Plan Usage page in the Electron UI with:
  - generic provider cards
  - current remaining/used values
  - compact credits and balances rows when reported
  - retry action for failed provider refreshes when the account supports reads
  - AO-aligned settings-style layout
- Adds sidebar navigation and notification integration for quota alerts.

## Scalability

- Provider-neutral domain and API keep the UI independent of Codex/Claude-specific payloads.
- Capability flags let the UI render whatever a provider can truthfully report without hardcoding provider names.
- Reads are coalesced with `singleflight`, and fresh account snapshots are reused.
- Storage is account-level, not session-level, so many sessions can share one provider subscription state.
- History is bounded and compacted; this is cached operational state, not an append-only billing ledger.

## Verification

- `npm run lint` was run; the full parallel suite hit unrelated adapter timing flakes, and each failed package passed individually.
- `npm run frontend:typecheck`
- `go test ./internal/service/quota ./internal/storage/sqlite/store ./internal/storage/sqlite ./internal/adapters/chatdriver/acp ./internal/httpd/controllers`
- `go test ./internal/adapters/agent/fake -count=1`
- `go test ./internal/adapters/agent/kilocode -count=1`
- `go test ./internal/adapters/agent/opencode -count=1`
- `go test ./internal/adapters/agent/primeagent -count=1`
- `go run github.com/golangci/golangci-lint/v2/cmd/golangci-lint@v2.12.2 run --path-mode=abs`
- Focused Plan Usage frontend test: `PlanUsagePage.test.tsx`
- `git diff --check`

## Notes

- AO only displays provider-reported values. It does not infer remaining prompts, tasks, or spend from token totals.
- Credits are shown only when the provider reports stable credit/balance fields.
- Claude structured usage is accessed through the ACP SDK's usage query rather than by sending `/usage` into a visible chat conversation.
- Quota history remains persisted and compacted for future trend/alert use, but this PR does not currently render an observed-usage history sparkline in the simplified Plan Usage card.

title: [Bug]: resuming an agent hard-fails with `can't find pane: 0` under a non-default tmux base-index
body:
## Summary

Resuming an agent fails permanently — with `can't find pane: 0` — for any user whose `tmux.conf` sets `base-index 1`. The tmux runtime builds its respawn target as the literal `<session>:0.0`, but tmux honours `base-index` when `new-session` picks the window index, so AO's own session has no window `0`.

`base-index 1` / `pane-base-index 1` is one of the most common lines in a hand-written `tmux.conf` (it puts window 1 under the `1` key), so this is not an exotic configuration. It affects macOS and Linux equally.

## Steps to reproduce

1. Put this in `~/.config/tmux/tmux.conf` (or `~/.tmux.conf`) and restart the tmux server:

   ```tmux
   set -g base-index 1
   setw -g pane-base-index 1
   ```

2. Start a session in AO and let the agent finish or exit.
3. Resume / restart the agent in that session.

Or reproduce it straight from the repo's own suite, no AO install needed:

```console
$ cd backend && go test -run TestRuntimeIntegrationSupervisedExitKeepsInteractiveShell ./internal/adapters/runtime/tmux/...
--- FAIL: TestRuntimeIntegrationSupervisedExitKeepsInteractiveShell (2.71s)
    tmux_integration_test.go:206: Restart: tmux runtime: restart session TestRuntimeIntegrationSupervised-d6de6f10: exit status 1: can't find pane: 0
FAIL
```

That failure is deterministic (3/3 runs) on a machine with the config above, and disappears the moment the config does — the same test on the same commit against a config-free tmux server passes. That is also why CI has never seen it: a default tmux sets both indices to `0`, so `:0.0` happens to resolve.

## Expected behavior

Restart respawns the agent in the session's pane regardless of the user's `base-index` / `pane-base-index`.

## Actual behavior

`tmux runtime: restart session <id>: exit status 1: can't find pane: 0`, every time, for the life of the install. The session is left alive but unusable for resume.

Direct probe against a tmux server with `base-index 1`:

```console
$ tmux respawn-pane -k -t "probe1:0.0" sh -c "sleep 20"
can't find window: 0
$ tmux respawn-pane -k -t "probe1"     sh -c "sleep 20"
(ok)
```

## AO version

upstream `main` @ `52fde0279` (`fix: hide inactive cloud sign-in controls (#4197)`)

## Environment

Arch Linux x86_64 (Omarchy), kernel 7.1.8, tmux 3.7b, Go 1.25.12. Not Linux-specific — the same `tmux.conf` reproduces it on macOS.

## Logs / extra context

Root cause is one literal, at `backend/internal/adapters/runtime/tmux/commands.go:24`:

```go
func respawnPaneArgs(id, cwd, shellPath, launchCmd string) []string {
	return []string{
		"respawn-pane", "-k",
		"-t", id + ":0.0",
		...
```

Every other pane-targeting builder in that same file already passes the session name alone (`send-keys`, `capture-pane`, `set-option`, `paneCurrentPathArgs`), and tmux resolves a bare session target to its active pane regardless of the configured indices. The file's own doc comment on `exactSessionTarget` spells out that convention; `respawnPaneArgs` is the one place that departs from it.

`panePIDArgs` (`commands.go:61`) carries the same `:0.0` literal but is not currently user-visible broken: `display-message` falls back to the session's active pane when the window part does not resolve. Verified — with `base-index 1`, `tmux display-message -p -t "probe1:0.0" "#{pane_pid}"` returns probe1's real pane pid, and an unknown *session* still errors, so the fallback is session-correct rather than arbitrary. It is the same latent assumption and worth moving with it.

I'd like to work on this — fix and regression test are ready. The test drives its own private tmux server (`TMUX_TMPDIR` + `-f /dev/null`) with both indices set to 1, so it reproduces on a default machine and on CI instead of only on a customised one.

title: [Bug]: destroying a session hands AO's terminal to one of the user's own tmux sessions (`detach-on-destroy off`)
body:
## Summary

If a user's `tmux.conf` sets `detach-on-destroy off`, closing an AO session hands AO's terminal client to **one of the user's own tmux sessions** instead of ending it. The AO terminal view then shows that unrelated session's output, and anything typed into it executes in that session's pane.

`detach-on-destroy off` is a common tmux.conf line — it is what keeps you inside tmux when you kill a session rather than dumping you back to the shell.

## Steps to reproduce

1. Put `set -g detach-on-destroy off` in `~/.config/tmux/tmux.conf` and restart the tmux server.
2. Have at least one tmux session of your own running.
3. Open a session in AO, then close/delete it.
4. The AO terminal pane does not go away — it is now attached to your other session. Type into it.

Reproducible mechanically, no AO install needed (fork a PTY onto `tmux attach -t <ao-session>`, then kill that session):

```
WITHOUT the fix (user has 'off') | client before kill: 'aosess' | after kill: 'other' | attach client exited: False
WITH  session-scoped 'on'        | client before kill: 'aosess' | after kill: ''      | attach client exited: True
```

The repo's own suite also catches it on such a machine:

```console
$ cd backend && go test -run TestAttachmentStreamsRealTmuxPane ./internal/terminal/...
--- FAIL: TestAttachmentStreamsRealTmuxPane (5.17s)
    attachment_integration_test.go:55: condition not met within 5s
FAIL
```

Line 55 is `eventually(t, 5*time.Second, func() bool { return a.isExited() })` — the attachment never observes the destroyed session, because tmux moved its client somewhere else instead of detaching it.

## Expected behavior

Destroying an AO session ends AO's attachment for that session. AO's terminal must never be reparented onto a session AO does not own.

## Actual behavior

Three failures, all silent:

- the attach stream never EOFs, so the attachment never observes the session ending and holds the PTY open;
- the unrelated session's output streams into AO's terminal view;
- **keystrokes typed in AO's terminal execute in that other session's pane.**

The third is the reason I am filing this as more than a cosmetic bug: it is input crossing a session boundary the user never agreed to, into a pane that may be running anything.

## AO version

upstream `main` @ `52fde0279` (`fix: hide inactive cloud sign-in controls (#4197)`)

## Environment

Arch Linux x86_64 (Omarchy), kernel 7.1.8, tmux 3.7b, Go 1.25.12. Not Linux-specific — the same `tmux.conf` reproduces it on macOS.

## Logs / extra context

`backend/internal/adapters/runtime/tmux/tmux.go` `Create` sets three session options after `new-session` (`status off`, `mouse on`, `window-size largest`) but not `detach-on-destroy`, so AO's sessions inherit whatever the user configured globally. tmux's default is `on`, which is why this is invisible on a default machine and on CI.

Setting it per-session is enough and does not touch the user's own sessions — verified:

```console
$ tmux set-option -g detach-on-destroy off
$ tmux set-option -t aosess detach-on-destroy on
$ tmux show-options -t aosess -v detach-on-destroy
on
$ tmux show-options -t other  -v detach-on-destroy
          # still inheriting the user's global 'off'
```

One wrinkle worth deciding on in review: tmux sessions outlive the app, so a session created before such a fix ships still carries the user's global `off` and keeps leaking until it is recreated. Setting the option in `Destroy` as well (best-effort, immediately before `kill-session`) retrofits those.

I'd like to work on this — fix and regression test are ready. The test drives a private tmux server (`TMUX_TMPDIR` + `-f /dev/null`) with the global set to `off`, attaches through the runtime's own `Attach`, and asserts the stream ends with no client left behind, so it reproduces on a default machine and on CI.

title: fix(tmux): resume an agent under a non-default tmux base-index
body:
## What

Address the agent's tmux pane by **position** (`<id>:^.{top-left}`) instead of by the hardcoded index `<id>:0.0`.

## Why

Fixes #4222.

tmux honours `base-index` when `new-session` picks a window index. On any server whose config sets `base-index 1` — one of the most common lines in a hand-written `tmux.conf`, since it puts window 1 under the `1` key — the session's only window is index **1**, so `respawn-pane -t <id>:0.0` fails with `can't find pane: 0` and **resuming an existing agent hard-fails for the entire life of the install**. Not Linux-specific; the same tmux.conf reproduces on macOS.

Visible in this repo's own suite. On a machine with that config, against `main`:

```console
$ cd backend && go test -run TestRuntimeIntegrationSupervisedExitKeepsInteractiveShell ./internal/adapters/runtime/tmux/...
--- FAIL: TestRuntimeIntegrationSupervisedExitKeepsInteractiveShell (2.71s)
    tmux_integration_test.go:206: Restart: tmux runtime: restart session …: exit status 1: can't find pane: 0
```

## How

The target has to satisfy **two** constraints, and the two obvious spellings each satisfy only one.

`:0.0` is deterministic but index-dependent — the bug above. A bare session name is index-independent but resolves to whatever pane is *currently active*, and `Attach` hands the user an ordinary attach client with tmux's default prefix key, so they can open a second window or split one at any time. `respawn-pane -k` would then kill the pane the user is working in and respawn the agent there, leaving the real agent pane behind as a corpse that `has-session` still reports healthy. `panePIDArgs` is worse: `supervisedProcessTree` roots its descendant scan at that pid, so a user-opened pane yields an empty descendant set and `IsSupervisedProcessAlive` reports a perfectly healthy agent as dead.

`:^.{top-left}` names the lowest-numbered window's top-left pane by position, which is both. `{start}`/`^` and `{top-left}` are documented tmux target tokens and predate AO's minimum tmux 3.2 (`tmux.go:750`).

Measured against a private tmux server — each alternative fails exactly one of the two integration tests:

| target | `base-index 1` | user opened a 2nd window |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `<id>:0.0` (main today) | **FAIL** | pass |
| `<id>` | pass | **FAIL** |
| `<id>:^.{top-left}` (this PR) | pass | pass |

Known ceiling, stated in the code comment: a user who splits the agent pane with `split-window -b` puts a new pane above/left of it, moving the anchor. Addressing the pane by the id tmux assigns at creation would be exact, but that means persisting new per-session state; positional targeting covers the splits users actually make. Happy to go further if you'd rather.

## Testing

Two integration tests, both driving a **private tmux server** (`TMUX_TMPDIR` + `-f /dev/null` + a cleared `TMUX`) so they reproduce on a default machine and on CI rather than depending on the developer's tmux.conf:

- `TestRuntimeIntegrationRestartUnderCustomBaseIndex` — sets both indices to 1, and asserts the window index really is 1 before restarting so a server that ignored the options fails loudly instead of passing vacuously.
- `TestRuntimeIntegrationRestartTargetsAgentPaneNotActivePane` — runs on **default** indices, opens a second window, and asserts Restart respawned the agent's pane and left the user's pane alive.

Clearing `TMUX` is not cosmetic: tmux only honours `TMUX_TMPDIR` when it is not already inside a session, so `go test` run from inside tmux would otherwise target the developer's real server and the cleanup `tmux kill-server` would destroy their sessions — AO's own agent sessions included. Reproduced that, then fixed it; the server setup is a shared helper so the second test cannot reintroduce it.

```console
$ go test ./internal/adapters/runtime/tmux/...          # base-index 1 box
ok
$ go test ./internal/adapters/runtime/tmux/...          # config-free tmux server
ok
$ go test -race ./...                                   # whole backend
ok
$ go vet ./internal/adapters/runtime/tmux/...
$ golangci-lint v2.12.2 run ./internal/adapters/runtime/tmux/...
0 issues.
```

Direct tmux probe behind the change, on a server with `base-index 1`, a second window and a split:

```console
$ tmux list-panes -s -t aosess -F "win #{window_index} pane #{pane_index} pid #{pane_pid} active=#{pane_active}"
win 1 pane 1 pid 402941 active=1        <- the agent
win 2 pane 1 pid 402944 active=0
win 2 pane 2 pid 402947 active=1
$ tmux display-message -p -t "aosess"              "#{pane_pid}"   # bare
402947                                              <- the user's split
$ tmux display-message -p -t "aosess:^.{top-left}" "#{pane_pid}"
402941                                              <- the agent
$ tmux respawn-pane -k -t "aosess:0.0" …
can't find window: 0
```

**Correction to my original issue text:** I wrote there that `display-message -t nosuch:0.0` "errors". It does not — on tmux 3.7 it exits 0 with empty output (`display-message` is `CMD_FIND_CANFAIL`). Harmless in context, since `strconv.Atoi("")` then fails, but the claim was wrong and the reasoning shouldn't be relied on.

**Overlap:** #4225 touches the same package. The two conflict only where both append to the tail of `tmux_integration_test.go`; `commands.go` and `tmux_test.go` auto-merge. I've verified the two fixes applied together are green on both tmux configurations and across the full backend suite, and I'll rebase whichever lands second.

## Checklist

- [x] Branched from `main` (based on `52fde0279`)
- [x] One focused change; links the related issue
- [x] Follows AGENTS.md conventions and PR hygiene
- [x] Tests added/updated for user-visible behavior where it makes sense
- [x] Relevant CI checks pass for the area touched (`go test`, `go test -race`, `go vet`, `golangci-lint`)

title: fix(tmux): stop a destroyed session handing AO's terminal to another session
body:
## What

Set `detach-on-destroy on` for AO's own tmux sessions, so destroying one detaches AO's terminal client instead of letting tmux move it onto a session AO does not own.

## Why

Fixes #4223.

tmux's `detach-on-destroy off` — a common tmux.conf line, since it keeps you inside tmux when you kill a session — makes tmux move an attached client to **another session** rather than detaching it. AO's terminal attachment is such a client, so destroying an AO session silently reparents AO's PTY onto one of the user's own sessions. Three consequences, all silent:

* the attach stream never EOFs, so the attachment never observes the session ending and holds the PTY open;
* that unrelated session's output streams into AO's terminal view;
* **anything typed into that view executes in that session's pane.**

The third is why this is more than cosmetic — it is input crossing a session boundary the user never agreed to, into a pane that may be running anything.

Measured directly, by forking a PTY onto `tmux attach -t <ao session>` and then killing that session:

```
WITHOUT the fix (user has 'off') | client before kill: 'aosess' | after kill: 'other' | attach client exited: False
WITH  session-scoped 'on'        | client before kill: 'aosess' | after kill: ''      | attach client exited: True
```

It also makes this repo's own `TestAttachmentStreamsRealTmuxPane` (`internal/terminal`) fail on such a machine, at the `a.isExited()` assertion — that failure is what led me here.

## How

Two call sites, covering two different populations of session.

**`Create`** already sets three session options after `new-session` (`status off`, `mouse on`, `window-size largest`); this adds a fourth in the same shape. Scoped with `-t`, so the user's own sessions keep whatever they configured — verified: with the global at `off`, `show-options -t <ao session>` reports `on` while `show-options -t other` still inherits `off`.

**`Attach`** retrofits it, best-effort. tmux sessions outlive the app, so a session created by a build without the `Create` hunk still carries the user's global `off` and would keep leaking until it was recreated. My first version put this in `Destroy`; review pointed out that only covers teardowns AO initiates, and misses the user typing `exit` in the keep-alive shell or killing the session from their own tmux. Attaching is the **exact precondition** for the leak — with no client of ours attached there is nothing for tmux to reparent — so setting it there covers an adopted session for every way it can end. That makes the `Destroy` call redundant rather than merely insufficient, so it is gone and four `Destroy` call-order assertions go back to their original form.

## Testing

Two integration tests, both driving a **private tmux server** (`TMUX_TMPDIR` + `-f /dev/null` + a cleared `TMUX`) with the global set to `off`, plus a bystander session standing in for one of the user's own. tmux's default is `on`, so a test relying on the developer's tmux.conf would be green on CI and prove nothing.

- `TestRuntimeIntegrationDestroyDetachesClientUnderDetachOnDestroyOff` — attaches through the runtime's own `Attach`, destroys, asserts the stream ends with no client left behind. It waits for the client to appear in `list-clients` first, so it cannot pass by racing the attach.
- `TestRuntimeIntegrationAttachRetrofitsSessionCreatedBeforeFix` — ages a session by forcing the option back to `off` after `Create`, which is exactly the state a pre-fix build leaves behind, then attaches and destroys. Fails without the `Attach` hunk, naming the leak:

```
attach stream never ended after Destroy; tmux clients now on: "ao-dod-bystander"
```

Clearing `TMUX` is not cosmetic: tmux only honours `TMUX_TMPDIR` when it is not already inside a session, so `go test` run from inside tmux — likely, for tests about tmux — would otherwise target the developer's real server, flip its global `detach-on-destroy`, and let the cleanup `tmux kill-server` destroy their sessions, AO's own agent sessions included. I reproduced that on a throwaway server (a session named `precious_user_session` did not survive) before fixing it. Server setup and the attach/destroy assertion are shared helpers so a future test cannot reintroduce either hole.

```console
$ go test ./internal/terminal/...                       # incl. the previously-failing attachment test
ok
$ go test ./internal/observe/... ./internal/session_manager/...
ok
$ go test -race ./...                                   # whole backend
ok
$ go vet ./internal/adapters/runtime/tmux/...
$ golangci-lint v2.12.2 run ./internal/adapters/runtime/tmux/...
0 issues.
```

Note: on a box that also sets `base-index 1`, `TestRuntimeIntegrationSupervisedExitKeepsInteractiveShell` still fails here — that is the separate bug in #4222, fixed by #4224, and unrelated to this change.

**Overlap:** #4224 touches the same package. The two conflict only where both append to the tail of `tmux_integration_test.go`; `commands.go` and `tmux_test.go` auto-merge. I've verified the two fixes applied together are green on both tmux configurations and across the full backend suite under `-race`, and I'll rebase whichever lands second.

title: feat(kanban): add prerequisites for future column derivation
body:
## Summary

Prepare the durable facts and live-update plumbing required for a later Kanban column-derivation feature.

This issue is **prerequisite work only**. It must not add `kanbanColumn`, alter board grouping, implement column rules, or add display statuses. Those belong in a follow-on issue once the required facts can be read and observed reliably.

## Why This Is Needed

The future Kanban reducer must answer two questions from durable facts:

1. Is AO currently responsible for internal review/fix work on this PR head SHA?
2. Did a fact change that could alter the future column, so the board should refresh immediately?

Today, the answer is incomplete:

- `review_run` facts are durable, but session list assembly does not load them as a reducer input.
- `review_run` insert/update does not write a CDC event, so the desktop only discovers review-run changes through the 15-second fallback refetch or an unrelated fact change.
- The compact `PRFacts` shape contains an aggregate review decision and an any-author unresolved-comment boolean. It cannot by itself distinguish an AO-authored review result from a human/external review result.

## Scope

### 1. Create a column-derivation facts snapshot

Add a read-only internal snapshot/query surface for future session-level Kanban derivation. It must provide, for every attributed PR:

- durable PR lifecycle facts, including current `head_sha`;
- current AO review runs matched by `session_id`, `pr_url`, and current `target_sha`;
- review-run status, verdict, trigger source, `github_review_id`, and the recorded automatic-review-injection policy;
- the session's `auto_review_enabled`, `auto_inject_review`, and `auto_inject_ci` policies;
- a source-aware view of external/human review facts when required.

Do not expose this snapshot as a broad new frontend API. It is an internal service/read-model dependency for the future backend reducer.

### 2. Establish source-aware review facts

Document and implement the exact reducer-facing rule for separating AO-owned and external review facts for the current PR head SHA.

Existing facts that can participate:

- `review_run.github_review_id` identifies the SCM review posted by AO;
- `review_run.target_sha` establishes whether that AO review applies to the current PR head;
- persisted `pr_reviews` carry review ID, author, state, target SHA, and `auto_inject_review`;
- persisted `pr_comment` rows carry author, resolution, and `auto_inject_review`.

The new internal snapshot must make it possible for a future reducer to answer:

```text
AO internal review/fix work for current head?
external/human review requires attention for current head?
```

It must not rely only on `PRFacts.Review` or `PRFacts.ReviewComments`, because those are aggregate values and do not carry review ownership.

### 3. Add CDC for review-run lifecycle changes

Add SQLite-triggered CDC events for `review_run` insert and update, for example:

```text
review_run_created
review_run_updated
```

Requirements:

- resolve `project_id` through the owning session and include `session_id` in the event;
- cover review creation, completion/delivery, failure, and cancellation;
- update any `change_log.event_type` constraint/migration required by the new event names;
- add the event types to the backend CDC vocabulary and the desktop event transport watched list;
- preserve the architecture rule: database triggers write `change_log`; do not manually publish parallel CDC events from store methods.

The current path can then stay consistent:

```text
review_run write
  -> SQLite trigger writes change_log
  -> CDC poller broadcasts within its normal cadence
  -> SSE event reaches desktop
  -> workspace query refetches
```

### 4. Make the read path board-safe

The board lists many sessions. The prerequisite query shape must avoid an unbounded per-card review-run/review-detail query pattern.

Choose and test one of:

- a batch query keyed by the listed worker session IDs;
- a session-list read model query that joins/preloads the necessary current-head facts;
- a bounded lookup strategy with explicit query-count coverage.

## Acceptance Criteria

- A future backend reducer can obtain current-head AO review-run facts without using frontend data or inferring from display status.
- The future reducer can distinguish AO-owned review/fix facts from external/human review facts; aggregate `PRFacts.Review` alone is not used for this distinction.
- `review_run` creation, completion/delivery, failure, and cancellation each create durable CDC records tied to the owning project and session.
- `/api/v1/events` replays and streams the new review-run events.
- The desktop event transport treats those events as workspace-invalidating events.
- A test proves a review-run fact change reaches the client via CDC; it must not depend on the 15-second workspace refetch interval.
- List-session reads remain bounded as the board session count grows.

## Explicit Non-Goals

- No `kanbanColumn` enum or API field.
- No `Building`, `Validating`, `Needs Review`, `Ready`, or Archive placement logic.
- No Kanban UI or Figma changes.
- No display-status work.
- No reviewer activity-hook changes. Review-run durable facts, not reviewer activity, are the prerequisite for column derivation.

## Follow-up

After this issue lands, create a separate issue to implement the pure backend column reducer, expose its result through the session API, and group board cards using that derived field.

## References

- `backend/internal/domain/pr.go`
- `backend/internal/domain/review.go`
- `backend/internal/storage/sqlite/store/review_store.go`
- `backend/internal/cdc/poller.go`
- `frontend/src/renderer/lib/event-transport.ts`

title: feat(telemetry): capture project GitHub org for usage ranking
body:
## What

Captures the GitHub organisation/account that owns a project so AO usage can be attributed and **ranked per org/account** (a prerequisite for connecting with the most-engaged teams and individuals for feedback).

- Adds a `github_org` property to `ao.projects.created` and `ao.onboarding.first_project_added`, derived from the project's `origin` remote.
- Parses scp (`git@github.com:owner/repo.git`), `https`, `ssh://`, and `git://` remote forms; returns **only the owner segment**.
- Adds `github_org` to the daemon remote allowlist for both events.
- Discloses the new field in `docs/telemetry.md`.

## What is intentionally NOT sent

Repository name, path, branch, or full URL. Only the owner slug.

## Privacy note (important)

`github_org` is **not anonymous** for personal repositories: there the owner slug is the user's own GitHub username. This makes AO telemetry non-anonymous for solo devs, which is why it is disclosed in `docs/telemetry.md`.

Follow-ups (separate PRs), not in this one:
- A first-run consent notice + a Settings toggle (recommended before this ships to users, since telemetry is currently on-by-default and described as "anonymous").
- Per-user `github_login` capture (needs the SCM identity resolver wired at the daemon root) for person-level outreach.
- Optionally hashing `github_org`.

## Tests

- `TestGithubOwner` covers scp/https/ssh/git forms, personal accounts, whitespace, non-GitHub, gist subdomain, and owner-only remotes.

## Risk

Low. Only adds one bounded string property on project-add events, gated by the existing telemetry consent/allowlist path. No behavior change when a project has no GitHub origin.

title: feat(telemetry): per-session token-usage ranking telemetry (on main's usage subsystem)
body:
## What

Emits **per-session token usage as ranking telemetry**, so AO usage can be ranked per GitHub org/account by spend.

This builds on AO's existing usage subsystem (`internal/observe/usage`, `internal/service/usage`) — which already parses agent transcripts (Claude Code + Codex) and persists per-session token totals — and adds only the parts it lacks:

- `internal/service/usagetelemetry` **decorates the lifecycle usage finalizer**. Right after the pipeline finalizes a session's usage at termination, it reads the session's usage summary, estimates a **USD cost** from a static per-model price table (Opus / Sonnet / Haiku / GPT tiers), resolves the project's **GitHub owner**, and emits one `ao.session.token_usage` event. Emission is best-effort and never affects finalization.
- Because ingestion is asynchronous, the event carries an **`incomplete`** flag when totals may still be catching up at exit, so you can filter or accept them in PostHog.
- `ao.session.token_usage` gets a dedicated **metering rate-limit tier (30/min, 1000/day)** so heavy users and orchestrator fleets aren't silently dropped by the standard 5/min ceiling, and is added to the daemon remote allowlist.
- Disclosed in `docs/telemetry.md`.

## Ranking basis

Group `ao.session.token_usage` by `github_org`; break down by `model`. total_tokens is a cumulative per-session snapshot, so take the latest event per session (argMax(total_tokens) by time) before summing across sessions — never sum a single session's snapshots. Cost is a query-time view (tokens x per-model rate), not emitted.

## Note on history

This **supersedes the earlier standalone parser/hook/endpoint approach**. After that was opened, a full usage subsystem landed on `main` (fsnotify transcript watcher + parser for both harnesses + per-session SQLite persistence). Re-implementing parsing would have duplicated it, so this PR was rebuilt to consume main's data and add only cost + github_org + the ranking event.

## Verification

- `internal/service/usagetelemetry` unit tests drive the decorator end-to-end with the real domain types: forwards to the inner finalizer, emits the event with correct tokens/model/cost/github_org, carries the `incomplete` flag, skips empty usage, returns the inner error while still emitting, and omits `github_org` for non-GitHub remotes.
- Pricing tests cover Opus/Sonnet/Haiku tier precedence, uncached-input preference, reasoning-as-output, cache-read, and unknown-model (zero).
- Rate-limit metering-tier tests (burst + daily ceilings). golangci-lint v2: 0 issues.
- Not run e2e: a full live-daemon path (real session termination → finalize → emit → PostHog). The decorator + wiring are verified by tests and compile-time interface satisfaction against main's concrete `usagesvc.Collector` / `SummaryReader`.

## Stacking

Based on `ao/ao-25/github-usage` (#4228) for the `github_org` attribution; merge that first or GitHub retargets to `main`.

title: Fix #3963: Bounded change_log + capped SSE replay prevents daemon CPU burnout
body:
## Summary

Fixes the high-daemon-CPU and intermittent write-failure path from #3963 by bounding both SSE replay and durable CDC retention.

## Root cause

Cursor-less EventSource connections replayed the entire append-only `change_log`. On a reported 722k-row database, multiple reconnects repeatedly decoded and marshaled the full log, causing GC and SQLite contention that could starve the single writer.

## Fix

- Treat a missing, future, or more-than-10,000-event-stale cursor as unpositioned and snap it to the current head.
- Emit an explicit `events_cursor_reset` SSE control frame before live delivery whenever payloads are skipped.
- Handle reset frames on desktop and mobile by refetching projections whose targeted invalidations were skipped; fresh mobile clients now omit `after`, and header plus control-frame reset notifications are deduplicated.
- Advertise the effective cursor through the typed `X-AO-Event-After` OpenAPI response header.
- Retain the newest 100,000 actual `change_log` rows, including across sequence gaps.
- Cap deletion at the atomic poller watermark so unread live events are never pruned.
- Run startup and six-hour retention in 1,000-row batches that release the writer between batches; acquisition is queued fairly so sustained writes cannot disable retention.
- Bound incremental vacuum work, use a passive WAL checkpoint, and add migration 0108 to prune and fully compact existing databases while enabling incremental auto-vacuum.
- Bound CDC shutdown waits by context.

## Verification

- `go test -p 1 ./...`
- `go test -race ./internal/httpd ./internal/daemon ./internal/storage/sqlite/store ./internal/cdc -count=1`
- Fairness regression: 10/10 normal and 3/3 race runs
- `go vet ./...`
- `go build ./...`
- `golangci-lint v2.12.2`: 0 issues
- `npm run api` with no generated drift
- Desktop typecheck plus event transport tests: 14/14
- Mobile typecheck plus full tests: 55 files, 459/459
- Independent Standards review: no actionable findings
- Independent Spec review: no actionable findings

## Evidence

- [Final published-head fairness, migration, and complete gate evidence](https://github.com/Untrivial-ai/agent-orchestrator/pull/4230#issuecomment-5393558391)
- [Published-head before/after SQLite and SSE reproduction](https://github.com/Untrivial-ai/agent-orchestrator/pull/4230#issuecomment-5392141394)
- [Complete-repair cursor, watermark, migration, compaction, shutdown, and race evidence](https://github.com/Untrivial-ai/agent-orchestrator/pull/4230#issuecomment-5392697087)

## Intentional scope

The issue author follow-up isolated the measured failure to cursor-less `change_log` replay. `model_usage_events` remains durable user-visible usage history and the issue defines no safe retention or rollup policy for deleting it. Existing age-based local telemetry pruning is unchanged.

title: feat(packaging): make AO install properly on Linux
body:
## Making AO install properly on Linux

Today most Linux users run AO by double-clicking an AppImage wherever it landed. It works, but AO never gets *installed*: no applications-menu entry, no `ao` in the terminal, and nothing keeps a deb or rpm up to date. This makes AO install like any other Linux app.

Plan: `docs/plans/2026-08-21-linux-native-install.md` (in this PR, with every step's findings recorded).

### What changes

**`ao` on PATH for deb and rpm.** The CLI and the daemon are the same Go binary shipped inside the app, but nothing ever linked it into `/usr/bin`, so `which ao` failed on a machine with AO installed and `ao preview <url>` was unavailable to every Linux user. Neither maker can carry the link in its payload (`electron-installer-debian` emits exactly one `/usr/bin` symlink; the generated rpm spec has a fixed `%files` list, so an extra file fails the build as unpackaged), so it is done with maintainer scripts in `frontend/packaging/linux/`. Each refuses to touch a `/usr/bin/ao` pointing elsewhere, and removal only fires on a real uninstall.

**No self-updating on a package-manager install.** `initAutoUpdates()` started electron-updater for any packaged build. On a deb or rpm install the app lives in root-owned `/usr/lib` with every file tracked by dpkg or rpm, so the updater tried to overwrite files it does not own. `isPackageManagedInstall()` (Linux, `APPIMAGE` unset, app directory unwritable) stops that, and the Settings panel says why instead of failing quietly. AppImage self-updates are untouched.

**A real menu entry for the AppImage.** `ao start` already wrote a `.desktop` file, but with `NoDisplay=true` — an entry deliberately hidden from the menu, which is why people hand-write launchers pointing at `~/Downloads`. It is now a real entry with an icon extracted from the AppImage itself.

**An Arch package** (`packaging/arch/`). Repackages the official deb rather than building from source: the deb is already laid out the way Arch wants, while a source build would drag a full Go build, a full npm build and a bundled Chromium download onto every user's machine. Adds a tracked `/usr/bin/ao`, restores `chrome-sandbox`'s setuid bit (without it Electron refuses to start), and installs a themed icon. `update-pkgbuild.sh` bumps it to a new release. Nothing is published to the AUR: that is a promise to bump on every release, and is a separate decision.

**Signed apt and dnf repositories** (`packaging/linux-repos/`, `.github/workflows/linux-repos.yml`), so deb and rpm users get `apt upgrade` / `dnf upgrade`. Both hosted on GitHub, no new service.

### Two constraints worth knowing about the repositories

- GitHub Pages rejects files over 100 MB and the deb is ~140 MB, so packages stay on Releases and only the signed metadata is published.
- This repo's Pages site is the landing page, and a second Pages deploy replaces the first.

So apt's metadata is uploaded to the release itself (apt resolves a package's `Filename` against the repository base, so they must share one) with users pointing at `releases/latest/download/`; dnf's metadata goes to a `linux-repo` branch served from raw.githubusercontent.com (it needs a `repodata/` subdirectory, which flat asset names cannot express), with an `xml:base` sending clients back to the release for the rpm.

Neither published package is re-signed — the chain runs through the signed metadata, which carries the package's SHA-256. Re-signing would mean overwriting published assets that the Arch PKGBUILD and the update feed pin.

### Verification

Everything below was run, not reasoned about.

- **deb** (`debian:trixie`): install, reinstall and remove; `ao --version` and `ao --help` work; the `/usr/bin/ao` link appears and disappears at the right times.
- **rpm** (`fedora:latest`): the scriptlet bodies run exactly as rpm runs them (`$1` = 1, 2, 0), including leaving a foreign `/usr/bin/ao` untouched.
- **Arch**: `makepkg` builds it, `pacman -Qlp` lists every expected path, and an installed build reports `0 altered files` under `pacman -Qkk` (setuid bit included). The app starts from `/usr/lib` with no sandbox error, an ACP chat session runs on the packaged Node runtime, the Browser panel drives a live page from the packaged agent-browser, and `pacman -Rns` leaves nothing behind. `~/.ao` is never touched.
- **Menu clash**: against a real pacman install, `ao start` resolved the packaged app, removed a planted stale AppImage entry, wrote none of its own, and left `ao-app://` pointing at the package's entry.
- **apt/dnf repositories**: built from the real v0.12.6 packages with a throwaway key and consumed in containers. Both install through the repository (dnf with metadata and package on different origins, proving `xml:base`). Both refuse a corrupted package, and both refuse metadata re-signed by an untrusted key.
- Frontend suite, `tsc --noEmit`, and `go test ./internal/cli/...` pass.

### Before the repositories can go live

A repo admin has to generate the archive signing key and add `LINUX_SIGNING_KEY` to the `release` environment; the recipe is in `packaging/linux-repos/README.md`. Until then the workflow fails fast with that instruction rather than publishing something unsigned. The one path not yet exercised is a real `apt upgrade` across two published releases, which needs that key and a release cut.

### Found on the way, deliberately not fixed here

- Release builds do not stamp a version: `ao --version` prints `ao version dev` from the deb published as v0.12.6.
- `frontend/forge.config.ts` passes `license: "MIT"` to the rpm maker, but the repo is Apache-2.0, so every published rpm claims the wrong license.
