title: fix(chat): recover rebound orchestrators and release stalled controller ownership
body:
Code changes: +437 -18  
Tests: +1396 -0  
Others: +46 -0

## What

Resume Chat conversations that still point at a retired orchestrator, and release controller ownership when output reads stop.

## Why

A project conversation can already belong to a replacement orchestrator while its active history branch names the retired agent's saved conversation. Resume then rejects the replacement's thread. A controller that stops reading can also block the persistent provider host indefinitely.

## Before / After

Tested main: `25bc9b148f`; tested PR app: `5160073564ff`. The app check used real Codex history in an isolated real dev Electron app. Normal clean replacement and Resume passed on main. To reproduce the older stored state, I staged only the conversation's active head back to the retired predecessor branch. I did not change branch rows or provider history.

| Input | Main `25bc9b148f` | PR app `5160073564ff` |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Resume with a matching active branch | HTTP 200; replacement thread retained | HTTP 200; same provider and recovery boundary retained |
| Resume after the staged old active head | HTTP 409; saved conversation could not resume | HTTP 200; saved history restored; replied "Resumed" |
| Cold and live recovery entry regression | Both fail: no boundary reserved | Both pass |

The app window was captured over CDP from the real dev Electron app. This is a staged historical-state reproduction, not a natural recurrence. No frontend code is added by this PR. The final head also merges main `23840aa541` (#7615), which changes cloud behavior and leaves the tested handoff, controller, rebound-recovery and publication code unchanged.

## How

The original fix uses read receipts to bound controller writes. It opens a new history branch only after proving that the replacement owns the project conversation and its saved native thread exists. The transaction checks ownership and history again before committing.

This update merges current main without rewriting history and adds a 70-line regression covering both recovery entry points. Added production code: 0 lines. There were no inline review threads or change requests to answer.

## Testing

Local backend build and focused race tests passed on `5160073564ff`. The same focused race tests passed again on final merged head `8ffc974b9108`. The same staged database failed Resume on main and recovered in the PR app. Both original branch rows stayed identical. A second exit/Resume kept the same three branches and provider identity.

- The exact same `TestReboundOrchestratorResumeEntries` failed on tested main `25bc9b148f` and passed on the PR. No existing test expectation changed.
- Full suites ran in CI on `8ffc974b9108`; all 20 checks passed. The first attempt timed out in `TestServerReportsIPv6LoopbackTaken`, added by main #7615. One retry passed without a code change. [Successful Go run](https://github.com/OrchestratorInc/agent-orchestrator/actions/runs/41558488649).

<details>
<summary>Local commands (Go 1.27.1)</summary>

Run from `backend/`, with `GOMAXPROCS=2 GOFLAGS=-p=2 GOMEMLIMIT=2GiB`:

```sh
go build ./...
go test ./internal/session_manager -run '^TestReboundOrchestratorResumeEntries$' -count=1
go test -race -count=1 -timeout=180s -run '^Test(ControllerWritePreservesSlowReaderAndReleasesStoppedReader|StalledControllerReleasesOwnershipAndPreservesACPReplay|AttachPreservesHostsWithoutProgressCapability|ProgressCapabilityRejectsUnknownOrRetiredAttachment|HostReconnectsSameProviderAndReplaysDetachedOutput|AttachedTransportOutlivesHandshakeContext|AttachHonorsContextAfterDial|ACPRelayReclaimsPromptAcrossAttachment|ACPRelayStallWatchdogWaitsOnTheClient|ReboundOrchestratorResumeEntries|OrdinaryOrchestratorRecoveryCoordinator|ChatProviderHandoffRequiresExactCoordinatorProof|HistoricalChatHandoffRequiresLatestCompletedMatchingTransition|RestoreTerminatedChatOrchestratorPassesProvenProviderBoundary|CommitChatSpawnRecoverySourceReproof|ReboundOrchestratorRecoveryPublication|ReboundOrchestratorRecoveryRepeatResumeIsIdempotent|OrdinaryResumeRejectsSameSessionHandleMismatch)$' ./internal/adapters/chatdriver/persistenthost ./internal/session_manager ./internal/storage/sqlite/store ./internal/service/chat
```

The persistent-host tests include 12,001 ordered synthetic updates, exact replay, an unchanged provider PID, progressing/idle readers, and stale capability rejection. The stall test uses a shortened 750 ms budget.

</details>

## Regression risk

Risk tier: NORMAL (score 1), no guard blockers.  
Could break: ordinary Chat resume, Terminal-to-Chat handoff, replay, and controller replacement for Codex and other Chat providers.  
Checked: real macOS Electron ordinary Resume, staged rebound recovery, a new reply, and repeat Resume; all passed on the PR. Focused persistenthost, session_manager, sqlite/store and service/chat race tests passed.  
Changed test expectations: none.  
Regression from: none identified. #7124 prevents new replacement identity mismatches; this PR recovers already-stored cases.  

Guard checks: the existing production diff is 455 changed lines across the two Chat resume failure paths. This update adds no production lines. The test-local `gosec` suppression names an AO-owned temporary journal path. The two comments flagged as commented-out code are prose, not disabled statements. Progress receipts run outside the host mutex; publication rechecks the recorded owner after provider I/O.

Not verified: a natural historical rebound recurrence, a desktop stalled-reader reproduction, a manual Terminal-to-Chat round trip, and native Linux/Windows app behavior.

- [x] Continues the original PR branch; main merged without force-pushing
- [x] Existing test expectations preserved

- [x] Focused checks passed

<details>
<summary>Original author's implementation and validation notes</summary>

The notes below are the original author's reports, preserved for context.

## Summary

Fix two failure paths that can prevent an existing Chat orchestrator conversation from resuming, without replacing its provider or rewriting historical identity.

### Release ownership when a controller stops consuming output

Bound controller-facing hello, replay, response and live-output writes with a 30-second no-reader-progress deadline. A fresh attachment-scoped capability enables read receipts over a second connection to the existing authenticated loopback listener. Actual output consumption renews an active write independently of the host mutex; there is no timer heartbeat. Receipts never acknowledge durable projection or discard the prompt journal. Older hosts that omit the optional capability remain supported. A controller that keeps its socket open but stops reading can otherwise hold the host mutex and exclusive attachment indefinitely. Expiry takes the existing detach/buffer/journal path and leaves the provider running. Successful writes clear the deadline; idle time and total replay duration do not consume the next frame's budget.

The socket regression checks that a replacement controller receives all 12,001 synthetic ACP updates in exact content/order plus the terminal result, using the same provider PID. This reproduces the failure class, not a proven historical incident trigger.

### Recover an already-rebound orchestrator's stale active-branch identity

Allow ordinary cold resume to append an independent provider boundary only when the project conversation already belongs to the sole live replacement orchestrator, the active branch belongs to an older terminated predecessor in the same project, and a positive native-history probe proves the replacement's stored thread exists. Provider resume must return that exact handle and pass native-history admission.

Publication atomically rechecks controller ownership, active head, history sequence, predecessor identity/retirement, source provider identity and competing live orchestrators after provider I/O. Existing branch IDs, owners, provider namespaces and messages remain unchanged. Same-session mismatches and unsupported or ambiguous recovery are not automatically healed. Recorded history with an empty provider identity is explicitly rejected.

Tests cover ordinary coordinator admission, same/cross-harness recovery, missing/erroring native proof, wrong provider handles, transaction rollback and ownership races, immutable lineage, and repeat-resume idempotence.

## Relationship to existing work

Related to #5218, which addresses controller I/O stalls with a separate output mutex and a five-second total replay budget. This patch uses the existing failure/detachment mechanism and a thirty-second **no-reader-progress** budget, so a progressing long replay is not disconnected merely for exceeding a total replay deadline. There is overlap in the transport portion; this PR does not incorporate or claim to supersede #5218.

Prepared on main at `994d609a9`, preserving #6270's `deliverProviderFrameLocked`/background-task settlement changes. The tested fork branch and running local installation were left unchanged. Local trial-only documentation and launch artifacts are excluded.

## Validation

title: fix(workers): drop parent-session identity markers from worker environments
body:
Worker processes inherit the daemon's full `os.Environ()`. When the daemon itself was started from inside a Claude Code session (agent terminal, `rebuild-ao.sh`, desktop app opened from one), the environment carries that session's own identity markers — `CLAUDECODE`, `CLAUDE_CODE_SESSION_ID`, `CLAUDE_CODE_CHILD_SESSION`, etc. Every worker then starts with a false "I am a child session" identity: the worker's own claude-code misreads the unrelated parent session as its own, with the follow-on behaviors documented in #2951.

This adds `internal/envfilter`, a small filter that recognizes the parent-session marker set, and drops those keys at the three places worker environments are assembled — unless the key was configured explicitly by the user, which always wins:

- `adapters/chatdriver/processenv`: the merged env for spawned chat drivers;
- `adapters/runtime/conpty`: the interactive terminal env;
- `adapters/runtime/tmux`: exec and attach env — the important one, because tmux's persistent server keeps the environment of the first CLI call for its entire lifetime, so one leaked marker poisons every later worker on the host.

Refs #2951 — this addresses the identity-marker half of that report (the "inherited CLAUDE_CODE_CHILD_SESSION marker" symptom). The issue's headline problem — workers inheriting `HTTP_PROXY`/`HTTPS_PROXY` and the inability to *remove* an inherited variable rather than override it — needs an env-replace design and is deliberately not attempted here.

title: feat(reports): surface delivery outbox state on the reports API
body:
Worker reports are persisted with a delivery outbox state (pending → delivered, with attempts and a last error), but `GET /api/v1/reports` didn't expose any of it: a UI could see that a report exists, not whether it ever reached its destination. The data was already in `domain.ReportRecord` — the API just projected it away.

The indicator polls through a small `useProjectReports` hook enabled only in developer mode, so normal boards make no extra requests.

This PR adds two things to Automations:

1. **Session-ended automations.** An automation can start when a worker session ends, not only on a schedule.
2. **Dreaming.** A built-in session-ended automation that learns how you work from what you type and what worked, and keeps your standing instructions up to date. Every new session starts with them.

## Dreaming

![Dreaming demo: three sessions, three dreams](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/OrchestratorInc/agent-orchestrator/66b03f88caa693e6c0fab214c6b33a5087b078ba/dreaming-full-demo.gif)

| | What you do | What the dream wrote | What the next session does |
|---|---|---|---|
| Setup | Turn on Dreaming under **Built-in** on the Automations page. Its edit dialog asks only for a name and prompt. | — | — |
| Session 1 | The agent runs the stale `make test`, then adds a `compose.yaml` to make Docker work. You ask it to remove that, skip `make test`, use `python3 -m unittest`, and show an example for this feature. | **Project:** "Run tests locally with `python3 -m unittest`; skip `make test` and Docker." Your example request was for this feature only, so nothing for you. | Runs `python3 -m unittest` straight away: no `make test`, no Docker. |
| Session 2 | "From now on, end each new feature with one example command and what it prints." | **You:** "End each new feature with one example command and what it prints." The project line stayed, since this session confirmed it. | Ends with an example and what it prints. |
| You | Type "Ask before adding a new dependency." into the box. | Nothing. Only that line is protected. | — |
| Session 3 | The team replaced the Makefile with `./check`; you mention it once. | Replaced the stale line with "Run tests locally with `./check`; skip `make test` and Docker." Your lines were untouched. | — |

Screenshots from the first version and CLI output are in the [dreaming evidence comment](https://github.com/OrchestratorInc/agent-orchestrator/pull/6716#issuecomment-6232691741).

### What you see

**Automations** keeps its usual screen: your own automations, or the empty state with **Create automation**. Dreaming is one row under **Built-in**:
- One switch turns it on in every project. The row says "Every project", or "On in 1 of 2 projects".
- Opening the row shows a selector, **You (every project)** or a single project, and one text box with **Save**. Edit it whenever you like.
- A status line under the box, such as "Dreaming updated this 1 minute ago · View session · Undo". **View session** opens the dream that made the change, and **Undo** restores the text from before it. There is no separate dream history; a failed dream shows its error on the row.
- Editing the row asks only for its name and prompt, and applies to every project. There is no agent or schedule field.

Every new worker and orchestrator, on any agent, starts with your instructions and the project's in its system prompt. A running session keeps what it started with.

### How a dream works

1. A worker in a project with dreaming on ends: it is archived, its PR merges, or someone runs `ao session kill`. Every ended worker dreams, including ones an orchestrator started and you never typed in.
2. AO starts the dream as a standalone background session, with no worktree and no setup scripts. Its prompt has:
   - the opening task, marked as possibly not yours, because AO records every brief as typed by the user;
   - what you typed after it;
   - the commands the agent ran and whether each passed or failed, without their output;
   - the exact commands to read and save instructions. `ao instructions show --json` includes the history of earlier edits.
3. The dream treats the instructions as everything learned so far. It merges duplicates, rewrites lines that this session refined, and replaces lines it contradicted. Lessons that hold in any project go into your instructions; facts about the repository go into the project's.
4. The dream stays out of sight: the board, sidebar, Archive and command palette leave it out, so the session you archived stays archived. It shows up only if it needs you.
5. With a chat agent, AO closes the dream when its turn ends, and marks the run failed if the last turn didn't complete. A terminal agent gives AO no reliable "done" signal, so it ends its own session. AO tells each one which applies.

Within a project, dreams run one at a time. A dream runs on the same agent as the session that ended, so dreaming never brings in an agent you didn't pick; it falls back to the project's worker agent only when AO can't read the ended session.

### Guards

Similar products have gone wrong in the same few ways:
- silent rewrites;
- lost user edits;
- one-off requests turned into permanent rules;
- prompt injection saved into memory.

I checked Codex memories, Letta's dreaming, Claude Code's auto-dream, Cursor's removed memories and ChatGPT memory. This PR guards against each failure:
- **Only you and dreaming can change instructions.** Inside AO, any other session gets `INSTRUCTIONS_READ_ONLY`. An agent that read a hostile file can't plant instructions in every later session.
- **Your lines are yours.**
  - Each revision records the lines you typed or edited (`user_lines`). A dream must keep them word for word (`INSTRUCTIONS_LINES_REMOVED`). It may rewrite lines dreaming wrote, even after you save around them, so stale lessons can be fixed. Editing a dreamed line makes it yours.
  - A dream must name the revision it read (`INSTRUCTIONS_CHANGED`).
  - Your own saves always win.
- **Dreaming doesn't re-add what you removed.** `ao instructions show --json` lists `removedLines`, and Undo counts as a removal.
- **It learns about you only from your words.** The opening brief is marked as possibly not yours. From a session you never typed in, a dream learns only project facts that the agent's commands verified, such as a test command that passed. It never copies instructions from files, tool output, web pages, issues or PR comments.
- **Bounded.** Each set is at most 8 KiB. AO keeps 100 revisions; `history` shows the newest 20 edits.
- **Precedence.** Project instructions win over repository files such as `AGENTS.md`, because they are newer. Neither overrides AO's own rules.

### API, CLI and storage

- `GET`/`PUT /api/v1/instructions` and `/api/v1/projects/{projectId}/instructions`, plus `ao instructions show|set`. The `using-ao` skill documents both.
- Automations gain `purpose: "dreaming"`:
  - at most one per project (unique index);
  - it requires the session-ended trigger and a worker;
  - an empty name or prompt gets the defaults.
- `ao instructions show --json` and the API return `history`: the newest edits, oldest first, each with the session that saved it and the lines it added and removed.
- Migration 0202 adds `instruction_revisions` and `automations.purpose`. Migration 0203 adds `sessions.background`, which the session API exposes. Migration 0204 adds `instruction_revisions.user_lines`.
- The Automations project picker no longer lists the Scratchpad, which holds standalone sessions such as dreams.

## Session-ended automations

### What

Automations can now start **when a worker session ends**, not only on a schedule. In the desktop app, pick **Runs → After a session ends** in the automation dialog. From the CLI, use `ao automation create --trigger session_ended`.

When you archive a worker in that project, or its PR merges, AO starts the automation's session about a second later. Its prompt is the automation's prompt plus details about the session that ended:

```text
This run started because an AO session ended:
- Session: acme-notes-1
- Title: Fix note ordering
- Branch: ao/acme-notes-1/root
- Pull request: https://github.com/acme/notes/pull/7 (merged)
- Task: Fix the bug where 'python3 notes.py list' prints the oldest note first; …
- Transcript: /Users/me/.claude/projects/-…-acme-notes-1/98eb0ed9-….jsonl
Run `ao session get acme-notes-1` for more detail.
```

### Out of sight

A worker started this way runs in the background, like a dream, so archiving a session never looks like it came back. It appears on the board only when it opens a PR or needs you. With a chat agent, AO closes it once its turns settle without a PR; a terminal agent ends its own session. AO tells it to attach any PR it opens with `ao session claim-pr`, so the session stays open even before AO's PR poll sees it. A session-ended orchestrator stays visible, because it coordinates workers over many turns. The demo below predates this change, so its review appears on the board.

### Demo

![Session-ended automation demo](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/OrchestratorInc/agent-orchestrator/d0d0807d5ae1b98cccb482d017d30116726db257/session-ended-automation-demo.gif)

[Full-quality MP4](https://github.com/OrchestratorInc/agent-orchestrator/blob/d0d0807d5ae1b98cccb482d017d30116726db257/session-ended-automation-demo.mp4) (1 min 29 s). This is one run of the desktop app built from this branch, with real Claude Code agents. The captions say where waits are sped up.

1. A worker fixed a bug in a small repo. Its AGENTS.md says to run `make test`, but the repo has no Makefile.
2. A "Session review" automation is set to **Runs → After a session ends**.
3. Archiving the worker starts the review **0.9 s** later.
4. The review's prompt names the ended session's task, branch and transcript.
5. The review agent reads the transcript, finds the `make test` dead end, and commits a corrected AGENTS.md line on its own branch.
6. Run history links the run to the worker that ended. Archiving the review completes the run and starts no new review.

Screenshots and CLI output from the same run are in the first comment.

### Why

People want an agent that runs *because something happened*, not on a timer. The first request was a "dreaming" agent: after a worker ends, read its transcript, find what slowed it down, and improve the project's AGENTS.md or skills so the next worker avoids it.

Today nothing fits:
- Cleanup scripts run on archive, but they are shell scripts, not agents.
- A scheduled automation can't know which session just ended.
- Cues are started by hand.

### How

- **What counts as "ended".** The hook fires from `sessionsvc.Service.RequestKill` (Archive, `ao session kill`, orchestrator kills) and from a new `MergedTerminator`, which wraps the PR-merge auto-terminate. It does **not** watch `is_terminated`. That flag also flips on daemon shutdown, agent switch, crash and spawn rollback, so a restart would start a review for every live session.
- **Which sessions trigger.** Only provisioned workers in the automation's project, excluding task-preparation sessions. Sessions started by a scheduled automation do trigger. A session started by a session-ended run never triggers another run, so a review never reviews itself in a loop.
- **One run per ended session.** Migration 0201 adds `automations.trigger_type` (`schedule` or `session_ended`) and `automation_runs.trigger_session_id`. A partial unique index on `(automation_id, trigger_session_id)` keeps it to one run per automation and ended session, even if the hook fires twice.
- **Overlap.** Scheduled automations keep their no-overlap rule. Session-ended runs may overlap, so two archived workers get two reviews in parallel.
- **Latency.** The hook queues the run and wakes the automations observer (`StartWakeablePollLoop`), so the session starts at once instead of on the next 15 s tick.
- **Context.** The prompt suffix is built when the run starts. The transcript path uses the same lookup as agent switching (`LocateTranscript` in the agent's own config home), so it still works after the worktree is removed.
- **Desktop.**
  - The "Schedule" field is now "Runs": Daily, Weekly, Custom, a separator, then "After a session ends".
  - With "After a session ends", the time fields are hidden and one line says what starts the run.
  - The list shows "After a session ends", with "Waiting" as the next run.
  - Run history links each run to the session that ended.
- **CLI and API.**
  - `--trigger schedule|session_ended` on `create` and `update`.
  - `trigger` and `triggerSessionId` in the API; the spec and TS types are regenerated.
  - An ENDED SESSION column in `ao automation runs`.
  - The `using-ao` skill documents the flag.
- **Telemetry.** `schedule_preset` accepts `session_ended`. Without that, the renderer sanitizer dropped the value.

## Testing

### Live: dreaming

The demo above is one run of a desktop dev build of this branch, with an isolated `AO_DATA_DIR` and real Codex agents. Beyond what the table at the top shows:

| Check | Result |
|---|---|
| While each dream ran | The board and sidebar showed nothing new; the Dreaming row showed "Running" |
| After each dream | AO closed the dream session when its turn ended, and the run completed |
| Dream 1 | It judged "show me one example command for the new feature" a one-off and learned nothing about you from it |
| Save your own line | `protectedLines` became exactly that line; the line Dream 2 wrote stayed the dream's |
| Dream 3 | It replaced the stale test line rather than adding a contradicting one |
| Codex in AO's default `auto` mode | Each `ao instructions` call needed an escalation, which Codex's auto-reviewer approved as low risk |
| Found while recording, fixed in this PR | As AO closed a finished dream, the session read "exited" for a moment before it was marked ended, and flashed into the sidebar under Scratchpad. "exited" no longer brings a background session into view |

Checked on the first version, with Claude Code and Codex:

| Check | Result |
|---|---|
| Next session, on Codex | Its session log has both `## User Instructions` and `## Project Instructions` |
| Undo in the project box | The text went back to empty and the line moved to `removedLines` |
| Write from the CLI as a worker, as a dream dropping your line, and with a stale revision | `INSTRUCTIONS_READ_ONLY`, `INSTRUCTIONS_LINES_REMOVED` and `INSTRUCTIONS_CHANGED` |

### Live: session-ended automations

I ran a desktop dev build of this branch with an isolated `AO_DATA_DIR`. Both agents were real Claude Code sessions: Sonnet 5.5 for the worker and the automation's default model for the review. Screenshots and CLI output are in the first comment.

| Check | Result |

| Archive a worker | The review appeared on the board 0.9 s after Archive |
| Review prompt | It had the ended session's ID, title, branch, task and transcript path |
| Review's work | It read the transcript, then committed `make test` → `python3 -m unittest -v` in AGENTS.md |
| Archive the review | Its run completed and no new run was queued |
| Restart AO with a live worker | No run was queued |
| `ao session kill` on a worker | A run was queued and the review started |
| `ao session kill` on that review | Its run completed and no new run was queued |

I did not run the PR-merge path live. `TestEndedHookFiresOnlyForArchiveAndMerge` covers it.

### Automated

- Dreaming:
  - `service/instructions`:
    - your saves always win;
    - a dream must name the latest revision and keep the lines you typed or edited;
    - a dream may rewrite its own lines after you save around them, and editing a dreamed line makes it yours;
    - `history` shows who saved each edit and which lines it added and removed;
    - removed lines are reported;
    - other sessions are refused;
    - the first dream can be undone;
    - the 8 KiB cap holds.
  - The SQLite store:
    - scopes stay apart;
    - a save on a stale revision fails;
    - an unchanged save is a no-op;
    - it keeps the newest 100 revisions, and the newest still carries your lines;
    - only human-typed messages count as yours;
    - commands that passed or failed come back newest first, never running ones;
    - `background` and turn states round-trip.
  - `dreaming_test.go`:
    - create defaults and validation;
    - one dreaming automation per project;
    - a dream is queued even when you typed nothing after the opening task;
    - the prompt says what the dream may learn when you typed, when you didn't, and for a terminal session;
    - each command is listed once with its latest result;
    - a dream launches as a standalone background worker on the ended session's agent, with the mode left to AO;
    - dreams take turns;
    - a dream without an agent fails;
    - AO closes a background run once its turns settle, fails it when the last turn failed, and leaves it open while a turn runs, when it opened a PR, or when the session is visible.
  - Real SQLite: one dreaming automation per project, and dream runs take turns.
  - `session_manager`:
    - instructions reach worker and orchestrator prompts from the store, and a standalone worker gets only yours;

    - one built-in row that opens to the instructions, with no delete action and no run history;

    - the dream status line, View session and Undo;
    - a draft is kept when the text changes underneath;
    - the switch creates or enables dreaming per project;
    - "Turn on" in one project.
- Session-ended automations:
  - `session_ended_test.go`:
    - It queues one run per enabled session-ended automation in the project, and none when the same session is reported again.
    - Orchestrators, task-prep sessions, unprovisioned sessions and sessions started by a review don't trigger. Sessions started by a schedule do.
    - Two reviews launch in the same tick, each with its own ended session's details and transcript, as background sessions.
    - A session-ended orchestrator launches visible.
    - It checks trigger validation on create and update.
  - `TestEndedHookFiresOnlyForArchiveAndMerge`: archive and merge fire the hook; an internal kill and a failed kill don't.
  - `TestTriggeredAutomationRunsDedupePerSessionAndMayOverlap` checks deduplication and overlap against real SQLite.
  - `TestWakePollsBeforeTheNextTick` checks that the observer polls when woken.
  - Further tests cover:
    - the API round trip;
    - CLI `--trigger session_ended`;
    - `AutomationsView` tests: create, the list row with its run link, switching triggers, and Dreaming kept out of the user's list with a dialog that edits every project's dream and has no project, agent or schedule field.
  - `telemetry.test.ts` checks that `session_ended` survives the sanitizer.

### Local CI on the final commit

- gofmt and `go vet ./...` are clean. golangci-lint reports 0 issues.
- `go test` passes for CLI, httpd, every `service/...` package, `session_manager`, the SQLite store and migrations, domain and daemon.
- One LAN-listener test, `TestLANManagerIdentityEndpoint`, failed once because another process on this machine took its port. It passed 3 of 3 times on rerun.

- Frontend: `npm run typecheck` is clean, and the touched test files pass, including the locale checks.
- After rebasing onto `main`, which added migration 0206: the migration ledger keeps 0201–0204 and 0206. Goose runs with `WithAllowMissing`, so 0201–0204 still apply on installs that already have 0206.

Not run locally:
- the full `go test ./...` and `-race` suites;
- the full vitest run;
- the docs build;
- the container smoke test;
- the Windows jobs.

CI covers all of these.

## Not in scope

- **One dream per ended session.** There is no nightly batch that looks across several sessions.
- **Agents' own memory.** Claude Code and Codex can still save preferences in their own config, such as `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md`, when you ask them to. Dreaming doesn't read or change those files.
- **No cap on parallel runs.** Archiving 10 workers starts 10 reviews. A cap that counts running reviews would stall, because a review stays "running" until it is archived.
- **Crash window.** If the daemon crashes between the archive and the run insert, that run is lost. Nothing retries it.
- **Other ways a session ends.** Daemon shutdown, agent switch, crash and project removal never trigger a run, by design.
- **Controller banner.** A background-started session opened in its first second shows "The agent controller stopped" until its chat controller connects. An archived Codex chat session shows the same banner, so a finished dream's page does too. Both already happen on `main`; this PR doesn't change them.
- **Terminal agents.** AO can't tell when a terminal agent is done, so a background run on one ends its own session. One that never ends itself stays open, out of sight, until it needs you.
- **Codex sandbox.** In AO's default `auto` mode Codex has no network, so each `ao` call in a dream needs an escalation. Codex's auto-reviewer approved every one in testing.

## What

Usage limits appear as a compact, neutral notice with a warning icon, local reset time, and countdown. Before reset, offer **Auto-resume at reset**. Once selected, keep **Cancel auto-resume** available while consent remains armed, including after the deadline during wake or transient backoff; show a localized waiting-to-retry state then. Show **Resume** when ready and unarmed, and remove the composer notice when a retry starts.

## Why

Quota refusals currently look like generic agent failures, and Retry gives no indication of when the prompt can run again. Users need a visible recovery action and an option to continue automatically after reset.

## How

- Expose a durable human-prompt fact on full and paged snapshots. Composer Resume/Cancel and earlier quota-failure Resume use it when the original prompt is outside the loaded history page; ordinary Retry and rollback retain their existing behavior.
- Recognize known quota refusals and anchor clock-only reset times to the original failure in the provider timezone. Nonexistent or repeated DST wall clocks remain manual; explicit UTC timestamps and trusted stored absolute deadlines are preserved.
- Normalize native Codex `usageLimitExceeded` refusals, preserve trustworthy in-turn UTC account reset metadata, and retain standalone quota errors on failed completions that omit the final error. Ambiguous metadata and display-only dates remain manual.
- Recognize Claude individual-spend/no-quota refusals and verify its native ACP terminal-failure extension through the real AO driver and persistent host.
- Translate recovery messages, controls, and countdown units for all eight supported locales.
- Persist opt-in consent and the absolute deadline on the failed turn; the daemon resumes it even after the view closes, the provider hibernates, or AO restarts.
- Reuse durable retry idempotency and recheck current lineage, delivery confirmation, and later work before dispatch.
- Consume still-armed, due consent in the retry-insert transaction, checking account history at that same boundary. Cancellation and account changes that commit before insertion prevent dispatch; manual retry remains idempotent.
- Skip per-turn validation until its stored reset time. Preserve consent through transient errors with 30-second backoff; up to four independent attempts can progress while other providers wake. The coordinator mutex guards bookkeeping only, and shutdown joins scheduled work before teardown. A 90-second attempt budget accommodates the existing 60-second wake.
- Keep earlier limited prompts manually recoverable after reset, preserving retry errors and avoiding duplicate controls for the composer-managed source.
- Auto-resume applies to a confirmed failed human turn with a known reset time; unknown reset times remain manual.
- Reuse the merged account service for a fresh, targeted quota read at the deadline. Shared native reset validation can postpone an existing deadline; a two-second best-effort probe never creates consent or replaces a trusted turn reset with an ambiguous display value.
- Commit account bindings and cancellation of armed consent together. Source-time binding history and retry receipts prevent scheduling an old-account or already-retried prompt.
- Use generated timestamp migrations `20261019220421171_usage_limit_auto_resume.sql` and `20261019220421514_usage_limit_reset_cdc.sql`, leaving main’s shipped `0213`/`0214` intact. Relocate only identified quota-preview receipts, preserving receipt IDs, saved prompts, deadlines, and consent; foreign `0201` history is retained.

title: fix: verify process ownership across recovery paths
body:
Code changes: +1186 -325  
Tests: +2272 -92  
Others: +25 -0  

Fixes #6695. Share OS process ownership checks across Chat recovery, desktop orphan-daemon takeover, native PTY/ConPTY cleanup, and managed cloudflared cleanup.

## Shared recovery rule

- Save the PID and OS start identity when a process starts.
- Signal only a matching owner.
- Reclaim only the old generation's record when the owner is gone or its PID was reused.
- Keep the record and block a replacement when ownership is unknown.
- On Linux, compare boot ID plus kernel start ticks; wall-clock changes do not change that identity.

Desktop takeover checks the exact observed run-file hash under an OS lock. Native cleanup retains launch ownership during recovery. Tunnel cleanup waits for confirmed exit, and an unresolved owner blocks only the managed connector until a later retry.

## Verification for this extension

Runtime evidence was built from `792b1e90ad23dccdf2108fc869c2fa6ac0166616`. Final head `dd7a1a0455ccd0c4e101a66c1a4259c688dacc47` changes only the Windows CI test selection and a deterministic test fixture; all runtime implementation files are identical.

- 21/21 real-process end-to-end cases: five Go CLI, eight native PTY, five daemon/tunnel, and three actual Electron startup cases.
- Ten complete affected-package Linux race suites passed; the Linux PTY shutdown regression also passed 20 consecutive race runs.
- PID-reuse cases preserve the unrelated live process; unknown-owner cases preserve the exact record and block a replacement. Reuse is emulated by pairing an actual old OS identity with an unrelated live PID.
- Five Windows targets compiled locally. The [native Windows ownership regressions passed](https://github.com/OrchestratorInc/agent-orchestrator/actions/runs/38957469520/job/117165226615) on the final head with Go 1.27.1, `-race -count=1`, including matching, reused, unknown and exited owners.
- Full local macOS frontend/typecheck/CLI/HTTP/lint checks did not all pass under severe host contention; exact failures, interruptions, and commands are retained in the evidence. Full affected Linux suites passed. All **23 CI checks passed** on final head `dd7a1a0455ccd0c4e101a66c1a4259c688dacc47`: [Go](https://github.com/OrchestratorInc/agent-orchestrator/actions/runs/38957469520), [Frontend](https://github.com/OrchestratorInc/agent-orchestrator/actions/runs/38957469603), [CLI E2E](https://github.com/OrchestratorInc/agent-orchestrator/actions/runs/38957469484), and [Gitleaks](https://github.com/OrchestratorInc/agent-orchestrator/actions/runs/38957469534).

SHA-256: `f05e3e2b67b87bc2d6bfd001e468536e7714296c55311575e5a69441c58a96a4`. Includes baseline/fixed observations, actual Electron screenshots, regression logs, source/build provenance, and checksum verification. <details>
<summary>Earlier Chat recovery and Linux clock-step evidence</summary>

Latest `main` (`df4cabc54`) was merged first. The Linux clock-step fix is committed as `0f95762ac`; its regression and API end-to-end proof are attached below.

## What

Resume recovers an exited persistent Chat host when its saved PID now belongs to another process, while other projects keep running.

## Why

After a restart, PID reuse made AO treat a dead host as a live owner despite its closed loopback port, blocking the orchestrator's Resume action. Fixes #6695.

## How

- Persist and verify the OS process start identity in host descriptors and launch locks at every host ownership probe.
- Share process identity reads with preview cleanup through `processalive`: Linux boot ID/start ticks, native macOS start identity, Windows creation time, and legacy `ps` dates.
- Preserve legacy Linux records while their PID is live because `ps` dates shift with the clock. Modern Linux boot/start identities still detect recycled PIDs; other platforms retain the legacy timestamp fallback.
- Hold a permanent per-session OS lock through stale-lock reclamation and host cleanup to prevent competing hosts.
- Cover legacy adoption/recovery, genuine and unknown owners, simultaneous starters, owner death, and recovery while another provider retains its PID and token.

The hello protocol is unchanged, so older binaries can attach to live hosts. After downgrade, an older binary fails closed when reclaiming a new JSON launch lock after host loss; the persistent-host ADR documents this limit.

title: fix(desktop): drop topbar and tab motion, keep tab strips scrolling
body:
Code changes: +48 -91\
Tests: +7 -4\
Others: +0 -0

## What

- The topbar no longer animates. The board label had a shared-layout spring, and the left padding sprang when the sidebar toggled. Both now change instantly. The settings page header shared the same padding hook, so it changes instantly too.
- Session tabs (terminal view and chat view) snap into place when a tab opens or closes, instead of sliding.
- Tab strips keep scrolling under a trackpad. Before, scrolling across the tabs would randomly stop.

## Why

The motion felt busy, and the tab strip scrolling was unreliable.

## How

- **Topbar:** `useTopbarPaddingLeft` returns a plain number instead of a spring-driven motion value. The header and label are plain elements.
- **Tab snapping:** `Reorder.Item` turns layout animation on by default. Both tab strips keep layout measurement, because drag reorder needs it, but set `transition={{ layout: { duration: 0 } }}`. The scroll containers are `motion.div` with `layoutScroll`, so positions are measured correctly while the strip is scrolled.
- **Scrolling:** the strip only handled vertical wheel input and left horizontal swipes to the browser. Chromium locks a whole trackpad gesture to the scroller it picks at the start, so a swipe that began slightly vertical could lock onto something else and the tabs stopped moving. `useTabScrollEdges` now handles every wheel event over the strip, on whichever axis dominates. All four tab strips use this one handler: session terminal, session chat, Browser panel and side chats. It replaces three copies of the old vertical-only handler, and the chat strip had none.
- **Terminal strip snap-back:** the effect that reveals the active tab depended on arrays that are rebuilt on every render, since file tabs carry JSX. Any update, such as terminal output, smooth-scrolled the strip back to the active tab. It now runs only when the active tab key or the set of tab keys changes.

## Testing

- `npm run typecheck` and `npm run typecheck:e2e` pass.
- Full `npx vitest run` passes except for tests that fail the same way without this change on this machine:
  - `ContextMeter` and one `ChatWorkspace` context-usage test fail under the `en_IN` locale and pass with `LANG=en_US.UTF-8`.
  - `browser-profile-import` fails locally because `better-sqlite3` is built for the Electron ABI.
- Updated the `CenterPane` wheel test: horizontal input is now handled by the strip and calls `scrollBy`.
- In the desktop app (isolated dev data), I drove real wheel input into the chat tab strip over CDP. Horizontal swipes, diagonal swipes that start vertical, and a vertical mouse wheel all scrolled the strip through its full range. Closing a terminal no longer slides the remaining tabs.

title: perf(desktop): make session switching instant with no layout shift
body:
## Why

Switching sessions felt slow. Sessions with the inspector open animated their width on arrival, the topbar actions slid around, and the chat replayed entry animations every time. A dev trace showed every click blocking the main thread for 580 to 830 ms.

## What changed

**No animation or layout shift on switch**
- The inspector rail uses plain CSS instead of `motion`. Motion applies even instant targets after paint, so the first frame of a new session showed the old width. Width and slide are now inline style and CSS keyed on `data-state`. A transition runs only for an open or close inside the current session (`data-motion="animated"`), and it expires once the slide lands.
- `useSessionSwitchSnap` sets `data-session-switching` on `<html>` when the router starts a navigation to a session. It clears two frames after that navigation renders. While it is set, the topbar reserve and compact-label transitions are off.
- Opening a chat no longer replays animations. A reply that was still streaming used to fade its whole last block in again. Text already on screen when the chat opens now renders plain, and only characters that arrive afterwards fade. The conversation scrollbar shows at once instead of fading in.

**Less work per switch**
- One `SessionView` now serves both project sessions and scratchpads (`LocalSessionHost` in `_shell.tsx`). Before, switching between the two remounted the whole session surface. The session routes now only match the URL and await the lazy chunk, and the previous screen stays up until it loads.
- Sidebar: rows get stable handlers, `ProjectItem` re-renders only when the switch affects it, and `SessionRow` is memoized behind the dnd-kit wrapper. That last part matters because opening a session refreshes its project, and dnd-kit's context used to re-render every sortable row. Components rendered per switch went from about 6,900 to under 2,800 in a dev trace.
- The keyboard shortcut dialogs are memoized and no longer re-render on every route change.

**Bug fix**
- The `_shell` loader treated a workspace fetch that a newer refetch had cancelled as a failure, which replaced the whole app with "Something went wrong / CancelledError". A cancelled fetch now counts as done. Real errors still fail.

**Safety for the shared SessionView**
- Session-scoped UI state now resets during render when the session changes: the reviewer, terminal target, browser and Files popouts, and the handoff dialog. Children never render against the previous session's values, and the handoff dialog, which never reset before, does now.
- A crash inside the session shows "Try again" (re-renders only the session, terminals stay alive) before falling back to Reload. The new string is added in all 8 locales.

## Not in this PR

The chat surface is still rebuilt on every switch (`ChatWorkspace` is keyed by session), and that is most of the remaining cost. Keeping recent sessions mounted with `<Activity>` would make revisits close to free. That will be a follow-up.

## Testing

- New tests cover:
  - rail settling for instant and animated closes, plus the expiry fallback
  - the switch flag lifecycle, including a late render and a superseded switch
  - the sidebar re-rendering only the rows whose state changed, including when the project's data refreshes (fails on `main`)
  - the shell loader with cancelled and real errors
  - the stream fade: settled offset, a chat opened mid-stream, a grapheme on the boundary, and text without a source position
- Frontend typecheck is clean, and the affected suites pass.
- Full renderer suite: the only failures are environment-related and unrelated to this change. `browser-profile-import` needs native `better-sqlite3`. Two `ContextMeter` tests and one `ChatWorkspace` test expect en-US number grouping.
- Reviewed in three rounds (correctness, adversarial, project standards). No P0 or P1 issues, and the P2s are fixed.
- Checked in the dev desktop app by switching with the inspector open and closed, across projects and scratchpads, with before/after performance traces.

title: feat(config): envRemove — project-configured subtraction from worker environments
body:
Workers inherit the daemon's full environment, and project `env` config can only add or override — a user cannot *remove* an inherited variable from a worker (#2951). The concrete failure: a daemon launched from a shell with `HTTP_PROXY` set forwards that proxy to every worker, and stream-based agents break against a proxy they never chose.

This adds `envRemove` to `ProjectConfig`: a list of exact variable names stripped from a worker's launch environment.

**Two layers of one mechanism.** #6710 (separate PR) ships the built-in denylist — known-bad parent-session identity markers stripped with zero configuration. This PR is the user-facing layer of the same subtraction: whatever else a project wants gone (proxies, locale oddities, ambient CI variables). The layers compose; neither depends on the other.

**Pins always win.** Removals are applied in `spawnEnvForOS` after the project-env merge but *before* the protected `AO_*` and PATH setters, so a configured removal can strip inherited values yet can never strip an AO-owned pin. Validation mirrors `env` (name grammar, case-fold dedup) and reserves the `AO_` prefix.

**Ambient names need runtime cooperation.** Map-level deletion cannot reach names that live in the daemon environ *outside* the merged map — a tmux server's inherited environment, the pty-host base, a driver's `os.Environ()`. `RuntimeConfig.EnvRemove` and the Chat start payloads therefore carry the list to each exec boundary:

- tmux emits `unset 'K';` in the pane launch command for names it does not also export (a configured value re-applied by the export is a pin and is never unset);
- the conpty pty-host drops removed names from its base environment (explicit configured values and argv assignments win);
- chat drivers filter their inherited environ through `processenv.Merge`, with overlay values winning.

Reviewers, shell/cue terminals and managed preview servers apply the same removals — their UI copy promises the project environment too.

Known ceiling: a tmux pane's *recovery shell* (after the agent exits) sees ambient values again — the removal scopes the agent's launch, not the server's lifetime.

Closes #2951

title: Reaper: sticky blocked/waiting_input prevents termination on conclusive ProbeDead (Cursor)
body:
## Summary

When a Cursor worker is in a **sticky** activity state (`blocked`, `waiting_input`), the reaper can report **`ProbeDead`** while **`isTerminated` stays false** indefinitely.

**RCA status:** **Confirmed** on upstream `main` at [`038547a74`](https://github.com/OrchestratorInc/agent-orchestrator/commit/038547a74) (2026-10-14).

Sticky states are treated as always having “recent” activity. `runtimeClearlyDead` requires **both** `ProbeDead` **and** `!hasRecentActivity`, so a conclusive dead probe **never** satisfies termination while activity remains sticky.

Stickiness is meant to block **time-based demotion**, not to override a **conclusive** runtime death fact from the reaper.

> **Evidence scope:** This issue is **code / unit-repro only**.

## Affected code (`backend/internal/lifecycle/runtime.go` on `main`)

```go
func runtimeClearlyDead(f ports.RuntimeFacts, activity domain.Activity, now time.Time, window time.Duration) bool {
	observedAt := timeOr(f.ObservedAt, now)
	return f.Runtime == ports.ProbeDead && !hasRecentActivity(activity, observedAt, window)
}

func hasRecentActivity(a domain.Activity, now time.Time, window time.Duration) bool {
	switch {
	// ...
	case a.State.IsSticky():
		return true
```

`ApplyRuntimeObservation` (`manager.go`) only sets `IsTerminated` when `runtimeClearlyDead` is true (plus launch/mutation guards).

## Expected behavior

If the runtime adapter returns **`ProbeDead`** (definitively gone—not `ProbeFailed`), the reaper should terminate even when activity is **`blocked`** or **`waiting_input`** (e.g. Cursor dies while paused on an AO permission hook).

## Actual behavior

Session remains **`isTerminated: false`** while activity is sticky and runtime probes are conclusively dead.

## Reproduction

**Code / unit level**

1. Persist activity `blocked` or `waiting_input` (e.g. permission hook under `default` permission mode).
2. Apply `RuntimeFacts{Runtime: ProbeDead}` via reaper or `ApplyRuntimeObservation`.
3. Observe no termination on `main`.

## Proposed fix direction

In `runtimeClearlyDead`: if `f.Runtime == ProbeDead` and `activity.State.IsSticky()`, return `true`; otherwise keep existing non-sticky logic. Unit tests; optional integration test: permission → `blocked` → dead probe → reaper tick → terminated.

## Environment

- Harness: **cursor**, `worker.agentConfig.permissions: default`
- Runtime handles: **`ptyhost-v1:<session-id>`** (no tmux on machine)

## Related

- #6727

title: Power-off: terminal ENDED and OSC flash while session stays idle/no_signal and not terminated (Cursor)
body:
## Summary

On Linux, a Cursor worker can show **TERMINAL ENDED** / `[process exited]` and a brief **OSC escape flash** in the embedded terminal after **full power-off**, while the session remains **`isTerminated: false`** with activity **`idle`** and display status **`no_signal`**.

Upstream reference: [`038547a74`](https://github.com/OrchestratorInc/agent-orchestrator/commit/038547a74) on `main`.

**Root cause:** Not proven yet — needs reaper/reconcile logs (`ProbeDead` vs `ProbeFailed`, and whether boot **`Reconcile`** ran vs the daemon stayed up through sleep).

**UI:** terminal pane shows process ended; summary shows **Idle** / **no signal**; session still treated as live.

## Screenshots

**TERMINAL ENDED** — terminal process ended, session not marked terminated (`Permission repro`, session 33):

![Screenshot 2026-10-14 20-47-35](https://github.com/LaibaFirdouse/agent-orchestrator/releases/download/untagged-0f8d9df25dcfbe8f697f/Screenshot.from.2026-10-14.20-47-35.png)

**OSC escape sequences** in the terminal pane (Referenced from `Cursor hook audit` session because `Permission repro`,session 33's couldn't be captured due to speed):

![Screenshot 2026-10-14 20-57-21](https://github.com/LaibaFirdouse/agent-orchestrator/releases/download/untagged-0f8d9df25dcfbe8f697f/Screenshot.from.2026-10-14.20-57-21.png)


**Session loads and Activity Idle** in the rail while the chat still shows permission / approval pause (`Permission repro`):

![Screenshot 2026-10-14 20-47-55](https://github.com/LaibaFirdouse/agent-orchestrator/releases/download/untagged-0f8d9df25dcfbe8f697f/Screenshot.from.2026-10-14.20-47-55.png)


## What upstream `main` does (relevant paths)

| Layer | Behavior on `038547a74` |
| --- | --- |
| **Activity observer** | Cursor is not a continuous terminal reconciler (unlike Muse). Reconciliation mostly targets **`active`** + stale output, not **`blocked`**. |
| **Sticky `blocked`** | `applyToolPrecedence` only clears **`blocked`** on turn boundaries or a correlated post-tool event — not generic `terminal-idle`. |
| **Agent `exited` hook** | **`ActivityExited` does not set `IsTerminated`**; reaper or explicit kill/shutdown does. |
| **Reaper** | **`ProbeDead`** → may terminate only if `runtimeClearlyDead` (#6726 if still **`blocked`**; if **`idle`**, must pass **60s** `defaultRecentActivityWindow` since `LastActivityAt`). |
| **Probe ambiguity (conpty)** | Dial **refused** → dead `(false, nil)`; **timeout/other** → `(false, err)` → reaper **`ProbeFailed`** → **no terminate** (by design). |
| **Boot `Reconcile`** | For live DB rows: if runtime is **definitively** dead → `saveAndTeardownOne` → **`MarkTerminated`** + restore marker. If probe **errors** → **leave session live** (`reconcileLive` returns error, logged). |

## Plausible RCA (needs log confirmation)

1. **`idle` + `no_signal` after relaunch:** `MarkSpawned` seeds **`idle`** and clears **`FirstSignalAt`**; `deriveStatus` can show **`no_signal`** after the 90s grace even when the terminal looks empty — consistent with restore/relaunch, not necessarily the permission hook receipt.
2. **Runtime probe not conclusively dead:** After reboot or flaky loopback, **`ProbeFailed`** (timeout) leaves the row live while the Electron terminal shows process exited (**UI truth ≠ reaper fact**).
3. **`blocked` → `idle` without terminate:** Not explained by the terminal observer alone for Cursor+**`blocked`**. Candidates: turn-boundary hook during crash/teardown, activity API update, **`MarkSpawned`** after partial recovery, or stale **`ExpectedUpdatedAt`** reconciliation. Needs logs: `reaper:`, `ApplyActivitySignal`, `reconcile`, conpty probe outcome.

**Evidence strength:** API snapshots + UI are strong; a single root cause needs **`ProbeDead` vs `ProbeFailed`** at reaper time and whether **`Reconcile`** ran vs daemon stayed up through sleep.

## Expected behavior

If the Cursor/PTY runtime is gone after power-off (terminal ENDED), the session should converge to **terminated** or a clear dead-runtime state **while AO keeps running**, not only on app/daemon shutdown.

Graceful shutdown **`SaveAndTeardownAll`** already **`MarkTerminated`** by design — “fixed when I quit AO” may be that path, not the reaper catching up.

## What to capture for investigation

One session id and timestamps; grep daemon/Electron logs for that id across the power cycle:

- Reaper facts per tick: **`ProbeDead`** vs **`ProbeFailed`** vs alive
- Activity state at probe time
- **`reconcile`**: adopt vs save-teardown vs probe error
- Any **`MarkSpawned`** / **`RestoreAll`** on boot

## Environment

- Linux (kernel 7.x), AO data under `~/.ao/data`, loopback daemon (port **3001** in testing)
- Cursor runtime handles: **`ptyhost-v1:<session-id>`** (no tmux on this machine)
- Logs often in the Electron Forge terminal, not a stable `~/.ao/daemon.log`

## Related

- #6726 — separate confirmed logic bug: sticky **`blocked`/`waiting_input`** prevents `runtimeClearlyDead` when activity **stays** sticky with **`ProbeDead`**

title: fix(preview): stop Linux previews after a wall-clock step
body:
Code changes: +74 -5\
Tests: +83 -0\
Others: +0 -0

## What this fixes

AO refused to stop a Linux preview server after the wall clock stepped (a VM resumed from a pause, an NTP step). It identifies a running preview by its launch time before signalling its process group (issue #3475), and it read that time from `ps -o lstart=`. ps derives lstart from the boot time, which moves when the clock steps, so the preview no longer matched its own record.

## How

- On Linux the launch identity is now the boot id plus the start in clock ticks since boot (`/proc/<pid>/stat` field 22). A clock step doesn't move either.
- The boot id matters because the process registry outlives a reboot: ticks alone could match an unrelated process that started at the same tick after a reboot, and the startup reaper would kill its group.
- The boot id is read on every check, so one failed read can't keep the daemon on lstart. If it can't be read, a new preview is recorded with lstart as before, and a boot-ticks record is refused with the read error instead of being compared with ps.
- The stat parse rejects a line without `)` or a non-numeric start time, as conpty's reader does.
- macOS keeps ps's lstart. The kernel stores the start there, so a clock step doesn't move it; a time zone or locale change still does, and this PR doesn't change that. Linux records in the old lstart form are still checked with ps.

## Testing

- `go test ./internal/previewserver/` on macOS, and on Linux (golang:1.27.1 container) with `-race`: pass. The Linux-only tests passed 20 runs in a row.
- New: the start time carries this boot's id and a non-zero tick count; a record from another boot doesn't match; an earlier process's record doesn't match a later process in the same boot (the #3475 case); an lstart record can still be stopped.
- Reading the wrong stat field (`fields[18]`, always 0) or dropping the ticks now fails three tests; before, the package still passed.
- `golangci-lint` for darwin and linux: 0 issues.

Split out of #6652, where it was found while testing remote previews in a VM.

title: fix(desktop): keep window transparency on after reopen, reload, and during startup
body:
## What was wrong

macOS only. With Window transparency on (Developer Mode), the blur often went away and stayed off.

- **Reopening the app.** On macOS, Quit closes the window but keeps the process running in the tray. Main stored the transparency flag once per process, not per window. When the app was reopened from the Dock, the new window asked for vibrancy, main saw the flag was already `true` and skipped it. The new window never got the blur.
- **Startup loader.** The renderer only set the transparency attribute after the shell mounted, and main only turned on vibrancy then. Until that point the window and the startup loader painted solid.

## Fix

- `main.ts`: reset the flag when the window closes, and apply vibrancy on every request instead of skipping when the value looks unchanged.
- New `lib/window-translucency.ts`: reads the saved setting and applies it from `apply-initial-theme.ts` before first paint. Main gets the vibrancy request before it shows the window. The shell effect uses the same helper when the setting is toggled. `ui-store.ts` imports the storage keys from it.
- `styles.css`: under transparency, the startup loader drops its background and shows the bare blur behind the mascot, instead of painting solid.
- `styles.css`: when a loader shows over the running shell (remote host loading, missing dependency), the shell is hidden behind it so the sidebar and panels do not show through.

## Testing

- Manually tested in the dev app on macOS: transparency stays on after reload, after Quit and reopening from the Dock, and from the startup loader onward.
- `tsc --noEmit` passes. Renderer tests for stores, theme, routes, and the native composition cascade pass. New `window-translucency.test.ts` covers the saved-flag read and the re-apply on every call.

title: feat: copy workspace paths and open installed terminal apps
body:
Code changes: +349 -43  
Tests: +387 -4  
Others: +0 -0  

## What

Add Copy path to the workspace menu, followed by Open in (Finder/file manager and installed terminals) and Open with (IDEs).

## Why

Let users copy the workspace path or open it directly in their terminal. On macOS, newly installed compatible terminals such as Warp should appear without needing an AO release for each app.

## How

Discover macOS terminals through Launch Services: select registered shell handlers that also advertise folder support. Open those apps with the exact workspace as a native folder-open event. Keep explicit directory launch adapters for supported terminals that need CLI flags, and discover registered apps outside the standard Applications folders. Cache terminal discovery and bundle icons in Electron main across sessions. Refresh only when the menu explicitly requests it, coalescing concurrent refreshes. Background state refetches and readiness polling reuse the cache without waiting on an in-flight scan. Editor and Finder launches skip terminal resolution; terminal launches use cached metadata with fresh file-existence checks. A failed refresh preserves the last successful snapshot.

Read terminal icons from their installed app bundles and render them to embedded PNGs in main, avoiding Electron's generic app placeholders. Installation paths stay in main. Finder, default Terminal, and Ghostty retain their bundled SVG symbols; unreadable icons have a terminal-symbol fallback. Reuse the native clipboard bridge and preserve the preferred editor when choosing a terminal.

macOS apps that do not register compatible shell/folder capabilities still need an explicit adapter. Linux and Windows retain platform-gated discovery and directory arguments for the supported terminal launchers. On Linux, the menu shows named terminals when available and keeps generic Terminal as a fallback only. The generic target remains callable for existing shortcuts and artifact actions.

## Testing

- 109 focused tests passed, including deferred-scan tests proving editor/Finder launches and readiness reads complete without waiting, cross-session cache reuse, concurrent refresh coalescing, explicit menu refresh, and removal/failure handling. Linux regressions cover GNOME with/without x-terminal-emulator, distinct named apps, fallback restoration, and generic shortcut/artifact compatibility.
- Complete frontend suite: 467 files passed; 7,849 tests passed, 6 skipped. Both frontend and E2E typechecks passed.
- All 83 renderer smoke tests passed in the CI-pinned Playwright v1.60.0-noble Linux/ARM64 container.
- Cloud client/product UI checks, docs production build, native helper tests and x64/arm64 builds, guarded-navigation integration, and Node 22.23.2 lockfile compatibility passed. Pinned Gitleaks v7.4.0 scanned all five PR commits with no leaks.
- Earlier native discovery/icon behavior was verified with a read-only macOS system probe; the user handles manual feature testing. Local native checks ran on Apple Silicon; GitHub covers Intel macOS and Linux x64.

title: feat(desktop): replace the New Task dialog with a new chat page
body: Code changes: +1793 -624\ Tests: +489 -1151\ Others: +223 -103 (translations, docs, DESIGN.md, generated route tree) ## What New task no longer opens a modal. It opens `/new`, which is the session's own chat before the session exists. The session is created on the first send, and the page hands over to it without anything on screen moving. - **Project:** picked in a tray under the composer; "Create new" at the bottom of its menu opens Add Project. ⌘N outside a project opens the last project you worked in, or Scratchpad if there isn't one. ⌘N on the new chat page stays with the project it shows. - **Agent, model and effort:** the same picker the session's chat uses, with its Agent, Model and Effort rows and its permission control, so the bar does not change at handoff. Picking another agent changes it at once; there is no session to switch yet. Locally only agents that can start are offered (installed, and signed in, needing no sign-in, or with credentials not yet verified), so "Auth unknown" agents are not listed. A remote host keeps the looser rule, since its readiness can be unknown with nothing wrong. - **Model:** one is always shown, and it's the one the task starts with. That's the agent's default when the agent marks one; otherwise it's the first listed model, which is sent explicitly. It's only remembered as your preference when you picked it. Cloud tasks keep main's rule (an unreported default is left to the cloud VM), since they read this device's catalog. - **On send:** the brief, settings bar and composer position stay where they are. The row under the brief reads "Setting up session" from the send, and the setup steps (creating the worktree, starting the agent) fill in under it once the session reports them. The session header slides into the empty strip at the top of the page. - **Rest of the page:** - Welcome suggestions are a row of short chips. Switching project with a draft no longer flashes them. - A paired phone with the app open shows in the tray. - The page has no topbar: the strip at the top keeps the header's height and drags the window on macOS. - Escape goes back, and the draft is kept. - ⌘⇧M opens the model menu here as in a session's chat. - **Composer, every chat:** the model and permission buttons no longer show a caret. ## Why The modal hid the chat the task turns into, and every handoff from the dialog to the session moved the composer. Starting a task should feel like typing the first message of a chat. ## How - **`NewChatPage.tsx`:** renders `ChatWorkspace` with a starting snapshot. On send it seeds the query cache (opening echo, launch settings, opening start time) so the session route's first frame matches the page. - **`useTaskLaunch` (in `TaskComposer.tsx`):** the dialog's launch logic, moved into a hook unchanged. `TaskComposer` stays as a thin wrapper for its existing tests. It also gives the page its agent list and an immediate agent change (`agentChoices`, `switchAgent`). - **Settings bar:** - The page passes `agentSwitch` to `TurnSettingsBar`, so it draws `AgentModelPicker`, the session's own picker. `AgentSwitchPicker` takes an optional `agents` list for this; with one, the Agent row is offered outside Developer Mode. - `chat-settings-template.ts` remembers the controls each agent's sessions report, so the new page can draw the same bar the session will. It falls back to the app's own controls whenever that bar couldn't show exactly what the task will start with. - `LaunchSettingsBar` holds the sent settings still, in the same picker, until the session's bar is ready. - **Sending:** - Only an answer from the daemon counts as a refusal. A lost response stays uncertain, so the composer retries with the same request ID instead of creating a second task. - A send made before the project and agents finish loading waits up to 10s. - **First handoff:** `React.lazy` suspends on its first render even when its code has loaded, so the first session opened from the page drew a blank pane for a moment. `_shell.tsx` now renders the session view directly once its chunk has loaded. - **Start-up row:** one slot from the first frame. Before the session exists, the brief's own group shows "Setting up session"; after the handoff, the session's setup steps fill in under that same label, so nothing swaps lines or text. - **`TurnSettingsBar` mode picker:** no longer adds a one-choice "Agent Mode" picker when an agent has no Plan-style mode. Claude's Plan toggle and OpenCode build/plan are unchanged. - **Transparency mode:** text drawn in the canvas colour keeps the solid colour. Before this, the send button's arrow disappeared. - **Backend:** `claudecode/auth_cache.go` no longer caches an auth probe that its caller cancelled. That cached "unknown" result marked the Claude catalog stale, and task starts that set an effort failed with "model capabilities unavailable". - **Backend, task naming:** a send while the prepared worktree is still being created reads the session before the workspace is saved. Main's background branch naming (#7069, #7085) re-reads the session before renaming, so the earlier fix here was dropped; a test (`TestTaskNamingAcceptsWorkspacePublishedAfterRead`) keeps the case covered. - **FX and agents with no default model:** the first listed model is shown and sent, so FX no longer routes natively. Main's FX test is updated to this rule. - **Follow-ups while starting:** a session started from the new page keeps the composer open during setup, so follow-ups queue in order. Sending does not shimmer the composer; its placeholder reads the same queue hint before and after the handoff. - **Setup checklist:** each step shows one plain-language label ("Preparing your workspace", then "Workspace created"; "Getting Claude Code ready") that shimmers while it runs; steps fade in one by one on a fresh start; the setup-script step appears only when the project has a setup script. - **Retry safety:** a send saves its project and exact request with the composer's pending delivery, so a retry after a lost response (even after a reload) repeats it with the same request id; errors that can follow session creation stay retryable; cloud creation passes the request id as its idempotency key through `createCloudSession` (the terminal fallback after an interface refusal sends its own key derived from it); fallback starts reuse their id until answered. A send is bound to the page it started on. - **Attachments, "@" and "/" on the new page:** the page uses the worktree it prepares in advance. That reserved session becomes the task's session on send, so "@" lists its files and attachments upload into it before the task exists. "/" offers the skills each agent last reported in a session. Scratchpad has no prepared worktree and keeps attach disabled. The file list polls until the worktree exists, backing off up to 15s. **Intentional omissions:** - **Cloud projects keep the New Task dialog for now.** A new task for a cloud project opens the previous dialog, which now lists only cloud projects; the new chat page does not list cloud projects. - **Chat/Terminal and display name:** no longer chosen per task. New sessions use the default interface from Settings → General. The docs are updated. - **Shared agent dropdown:** the dropdown used in project creation, project settings and the cloud New Task dialog is unchanged; it still offers "Auth unknown" agents by main's design (#5921). Cloud agents are always signed in or not, so the label cannot appear in the cloud dialog. - **README screenshot (`new-task.png`):** still shows the old dialog and needs a fresh capture. ## Testing - `npx tsc --noEmit` and `npx tsc --noEmit -p tsconfig.e2e.json` pass. Backend builds; `session_manager` and `claudecode` tests pass. - **Full frontend unit suite:** run on this branch. Failures are machine-only and also fail on `main` here: `browser-profile-import` (native module built for Electron), `auto-updater` (timing-flaky), and two locale-dependent context-meter tests. - **e2e:** `new-chat-handoff`, `new-task-focus`, `cross-platform-focus` and `model-menu-scroll`, 19 tests, pass. New coverage: no blank frame on the first handoff, ⌘⇧M on the new page and in a chat, switching project with a draft never flashes the suggestions; unit tests for the agent list ("Auth unknown" never offered locally) and ⌘N on the new page. Each new test was checked to fail without its fix. - **Verified in the isolated desktop dev app:** the handoff from the new page to the session, the shared settings bar, the tray, the chips, the topbar strip, transparency mode, and the phone indicator. ## Checklist - [x] Branched from `main` (or continuing an existing PR branch) - [x] One focused change; links the related issue when applicable - [x] Follows [AGENTS.md](https://github.com/Untrivial-ai/agent-orchestrator/blob/main/AGENTS.md) conventions and PR hygiene - [x] Tests added/updated for user-visible behavior where it makes sense - [x] Relevant CI checks pass for the area touched (`go`, frontend, etc.) 🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code) https://claude.ai/code/session_01FqhR6iFmGCnAPsqzutAxUS

title: feat(cli): add setup-token option to local Claude Code login
body:
## Summary
- Adds option 4 **Setup token** to AO's local Claude Code login menu. The user runs `claude setup-token` and pastes the result. Input is hidden, checked against `sk-ant-oat…`, zeroed after use, and saved atomically (temp file + rename, mode 0600, directory 0700) to its own file, `AO_DATA_DIR/harnesses/claude-code/setup-token`, via `claudecode.SaveLocalOAuthToken`.
- **Latest login wins.** Choosing the setup token is an explicit sign-in, so local sessions get it as `CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN` even when Claude Code has its own native login. Signing in through options 1–3 deletes the saved token, so the newer login takes over. A credential set for the launch itself (project env `CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN` / `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` / `ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN`, or an account `CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR`) still beats the machine-wide token.
- **The AO Cloud token never shadows a native login.** The desktop app's AO Cloud sign-in writes a separate token, `harnesses/claude-code/oauth-token`. Nobody chose it for local work, so it keeps the original #5878 guard: it's injected only when Claude Code has no first-party login (env, Claude settings env, credentials file, keychain). Options 1–3 leave it alone. Tokens saved by older builds stay on this safe rule after upgrading.
- **Readiness and provider-switch checks agree with launch.** A new `ports.AgentRuntimeAuthChecker` (`AuthStatusForRuntime(ctx, dataDir)`) applies `AugmentRuntimeEnv` before running the normal auth ladder. The readiness coordinator and the TUI provider-switch preflight both use it, so a machine whose only credential is the setup token shows as signed in and can switch to Claude Code. Account identity, diagnostics and verdict caching are unchanged; the cache is keyed by credential fingerprint.
- **Model discovery and the computer's account see the token too.** A new optional `ports.AgentRuntimeCredentialEnv` (`RuntimeCredentialEnv(dataDir)`), implemented by the Claude plugin from `AugmentRuntimeEnv`, is applied to:
  - local model-catalog discovery, which previously found no credential on a token-only machine, left the catalog stale, and failed explicit models with `MODEL_CAPABILITIES_UNAVAILABLE`;
  - the "this computer" Claude account's CLI checks, which previously read the account as signed out and refused new sessions with `AGENT_ACCOUNT_DEFAULT_UNUSABLE`.
  Account folders and cloud credential scopes are unchanged.
- The login terminal gets the daemon's resolved absolute `AO_DATA_DIR`, so a relative override can't save the token inside the temporary auth workspace.
- Updates menu/plan guidance text.

## Tests (run in CI)
- `cli`: token saved and not echoed; invalid token rejected and not saved; options 1–3 remove a saved token.
- `claudecode`: token injection, launch-env precedence, account-launch skip, real probe with the saved token, atomic replace, `RuntimeCredentialEnv`.
- `agent` readiness: runtime checker is used when a data dir is set; accepted, rejected and unverified tokens.
- `agent` catalog: local discovery carries the saved token; cloud credential scopes do not.
- `agentaccount`: the computer's account reads as signed in with the saved token; an account folder does not.
- `session_manager`: switch preflight routes through the runtime checker.
- `agentauth`: plan text and absolute `AO_DATA_DIR` handoff.

## Manual end-to-end (Linux VPS, no native Claude login, Claude Code 2.1.284, commit `9bd87e54e1`)
| Check | Result |
|---|---|
| Option 4 saves a real token (0600 file, 0700 dir, never printed) | Pass |
| Invalid token rejected (exit 2, saved file unchanged) | Pass |
| Daemon readiness reports Claude Code authorized | Pass |
| Model catalog lists 14 models, not stale; explicit `claude-haiku-4-5` worker replies | Pass |
| "This computer" account signed in; four sequential workers launch on it | Pass |
| Worker process has `CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN` | Pass |
| Project `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` beats the token (token not injected, key used) | Pass |
| Token absent from all daemon and test logs | Pass |

## Risks
- Saved tokens are plaintext on disk (0600) under the AO data dir.
- Because the menu's token beats a native login, a user who chose it and later signs in natively **outside** AO keeps using the token until they sign in through AO's menu (options 1–3). If the token is revoked, readiness reports it as signed out, which points them back to that menu.
- Setup tokens are inference-only, so Claude features that need a full login (Remote Control, Claude in Chrome) do not work with one.
- AO checks only the session's own env for a competing credential. An `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` / `ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN` in the daemon's own environment still reaches sessions, and Claude Code prefers it over the token.

title: docs: explain the contributor process for bugs and features
body:
Code changes: +0 -0
