title: feat(daemon): hold an exclusive data-dir lock so two daemons never share ao.db
body:
Code changes: +317 -4  
Tests: +318 -0  
Others: +7 -4 (Windows CI step, ao-desktop-dev skill, `AO_SHUTDOWN_TIMEOUT` docs)

## Impact

| | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| Two daemons writing `ao.db` at once during a desktop takeover (3 reps) | **9.90 s** of overlap | **0 s** |
| Second daemon started on the same data dir | opens `ao.db` and serves next to the first | never opens it; exits 75 after 108 s |
| Successor waiting when the holder is SIGKILLed | n/a | takes the lock in 0.088 s |

## What

Only one AO process can own a data dir now. Before it opens SQLite, the daemon takes an exclusive OS lock on `<AO_DATA_DIR>/daemon.lock`: `flock` on macOS and Linux, `LockFileEx` on Windows. It holds the lock until it exits, and the OS drops it on any exit, SIGKILL included.

- A daemon that finds the lock held logs that it is waiting and retries for 9 x `AO_SHUTDOWN_TIMEOUT` + 18 s (108 s by default). If the lock is still held, it exits with code **75** and this message:
  `data dir is in use by another AO process: <dir> (pid N); waited 1m48s for it to exit, refusing to start`
- `ao import` takes the same lock. When it is held, the import refuses with a usage error (exit 2) that names the holder's PID, before it opens `ao.db`.
- On a file system that cannot lock files (some NFS, SMB and FUSE mounts: `ENOTSUP`, `EOPNOTSUPP` or `ENOLCK` from `flock`; `ERROR_NOT_SUPPORTED` or `ERROR_INVALID_FUNCTION` from `LockFileEx`), the daemon logs a warning and starts without the lock, and `ao import` relies on its run-file check, as both did before this change.

This takes over draft #5407 by @Pulkit7070. His commit (the `datadirlock` package, locking before `sqlite.Open`) is kept unchanged with his authorship. The later commits build on it.

## Why

Issue #3716: a second daemon on the same `AO_DATA_DIR` hot-migrated `ao.db` under a running daemon. The first daemon's prepared statements stopped matching the schema, and Run review failed with `REVIEW_OPERATION_FAILED`. Nothing prevented this:

- The startup guard checks only `AO_RUN_FILE` and `AO_PORT`.
- `running.json` is written after migrations.
- The port is not a mutex: `EADDRINUSE` falls back to an ephemeral port.
- `ao import` opened and migrated the DB behind only a PID-alive check.

#5407's lock fails fast, which is not enough for the desktop. The desktop's takeover (`gracefullyReplaceDaemonForBrowser`, and the wedged-orphan path in `startDaemonInner`) spawns the new daemon as soon as the old one's `/healthz` stops answering. `http.Server.Shutdown` closes the listener first, so `/healthz` goes dark about 0.06 s after `POST /shutdown`. The old process then keeps `ao.db` open while it drains requests and stops workers. A fail-fast lock would make the new daemon exit during a routine relaunch.

## How

- `datadirlock.Acquire(ctx, dataDir, wait)` retries every 100 ms until `wait` elapses. Neither `flock` nor `LockFileEx` can block with a timeout, so polling is the portable way to bound the wait. The returned error wraps `ErrLocked` and names the holder's PID, which is read from the lock file.
- **The wait bound is `9T + 18 s`, with T = `ShutdownTimeout`: 108 s by default.** Once the old daemon's `/healthz` goes dark, its capped shutdown (the end of `daemon.Run`) takes at most **8T + 18 s**:
  - The HTTP drain, T. Any open `/api/v1/events` stream holds it for the full 10 s; measured exit was 10.02 s after `/shutdown`.
  - Seven stages capped at T each: failure dispatcher, harness installer, background workers, agent-switch workers, Codex account-switch workers, chat `StopAll`, and the LAN listener.
  - Fixed caps:
    - a 5 s agent-switch fault enqueue, only when those workers time out;
    - a 3 s `tailscale serve off`, when Secure Pairing is on or a serve cleanup is pending;
    - a 5 s closed-lid lease release plus a 3 s caffeinate exit, with keep-awake on (the lease poll is new in `main`'s `LidAwake.Stop`);
    - a 2 s Sentry flush.

  The extra T is margin. `Run`'s uncapped waits are not covered; see "Not covered". The bound scales only with the existing `AO_SHUTDOWN_TIMEOUT`; there is no new setting, and the three user-facing docs that describe that variable now mention it. `restartDaemon` already waits for the old child to exit, so it never waits on the lock.
- **What the desktop shows during the wait.** The full-screen startup screen (the mascot), with no message, until the old daemon exits and the new one is ready. The desktop sets its "AO daemon is still starting" status 30 s after spawn, but the startup screen does not render that status, so the waiting line appears only in the daemon output. If the wait runs out, the daemon exits 75 and the desktop shows its error banner with the output.
- **Exit code 75** (`EX_TEMPFAIL`) comes from `cli.ExitCode` when the error wraps `datadirlock.ErrLocked`. It separates a refused start from a crash (exit 1). The desktop needs no change: it already reports "Daemon exited with code 75" with the daemon's output, including the message above, in the details.
- **`ao import`** takes the lock right before `sqlite.Open` and does not wait. Its existing run-file check misses a daemon that has its own `AO_RUN_FILE`, or one still starting that has not written its run-file yet. Plain `ao stop` cannot reach such a daemon, so the refusal names the holder's PID instead.
- Only a lock that is still held produces the "refusing to start" message and exit 75. Any other error while waiting, such as I/O, comes back as itself and exits 1.
- **Windows** locks one byte at offset 1 GiB instead of byte 0. Windows range locks are mandatory, so locking byte 0 hid the holder's PID from a contender.
- The lock file is created with mode 0600 (gosec), and the data dir is created if missing. The diagnostic PID write no longer fsyncs. On darwin that was an `F_FULLFSYNC` on every start: 4 ms median, up to 23 ms, measured here.
- `os.OpenFile` is close-on-exec, so tmux servers and chat hosts that outlive the daemon never inherit the lock.
- The lock is released after `store.Close`, at the end of `daemon.Run`.
- CI: the `windows-workspace` job now runs the `datadirlock` tests. The CLI e2e matrix (ubuntu, macos, windows) runs two real daemons on one data dir.
- `.agents/skills/ao-desktop-dev`: real-data mode now has to quit the packaged app first, because the dev daemon would wait and then exit 75.

## Evidence

Measured on a Mac15,6 (M3 Pro), macOS 26.5.1, Go 1.27.1, on AC power:
- Base binary `df4cabc544`. Branch binary `e84248df26` (final) for the first row; `9eddae46b3` (the same lock code before the rebase) for the other two, whose numbers do not depend on the wait bound.
- Each daemon runs as `ao daemon` in a scratch data dir under `sandbox-exec`, with isolated `HOME`, a free port, and telemetry off.
- `ao.db` holders are read with `lsof -p`. Exit times come from `waitpid`; lock times from the daemon's own log.
- `caffeinate` plus a wall-vs-monotonic sleep guard was used: no repetition slept.
- Results are median [min-max].

| Scenario | base | branch |
|---|---|---|
| **Second daemon, own port and run-file, same data dir** (3 reps) | serves, ready in 0.48 s; both PIDs hold `ao.db` in 10/10 samples; writes its own run-file | logs that it waits at 0.047 s, exits **75** at 108.15 s [108.07-108.15]; never opens `ao.db` (0 of 654 samples); first daemon keeps serving |
| **Takeover of a draining daemon** (3 reps): `POST /shutdown`, spawn when `/healthz` goes dark (0.06 s) | old daemon exits at 10.02 s, new one holds `ao.db` from 0.12 s; **two writers for 9.90 s [9.86-9.90]** | new one takes the lock at 10.12 s, 0.074 s [0.040-0.080] after the old one exits; ready at 10.29 s; **0 s overlap**, 0 of 87 samples with both |
| **SIGKILL of the holder while a successor waits** (5 reps) | n/a (no lock) | lock acquired 0.088 s [0.083-0.100] after SIGKILL; ready at 0.17 s |

Not measured locally: Windows and Linux (CI covers them), the Electron app itself (the takeover repeats its HTTP sequence), and a real-size DB.

## Testing

The last commit, `b1afee2ec3` (start without the lock where the file system cannot lock, plus `TestLockErrorSeparatesHeldFromUnsupported` for unix and Windows), was rebased onto `origin/main` and was not run locally; remote CI covers it. Everything below ran on the earlier head.

Final runs, all on `e84248df26` (rebased on `origin/main` @ `a4d6e48eec`):
- `go test -race -count=1 -p 4 -v ./internal/datadirlock/ ./internal/daemon/`, unfiltered: pass.
- `go test -race -count=1 -v ./internal/cli/ -run 'TestImportCommand|TestExitCodeDataDirLocked'`: pass.
- `go test -count=1 -tags e2e -v -run 'TestE2E_SecondDaemonOnSameDataDir$' ./internal/cli/` on macOS, with a CI-like env (minimal `PATH`, isolated `HOME`): pass, 21.1 s. The refused daemon runs under a 35 s deadline; `AO_SHUTDOWN_TIMEOUT=100ms` gives an 18.9 s wait.
- `go test -count=1 -p 4 ./...` in a CI-like env (isolated `HOME`, no ambient `CLAUDE_CODE_*` variables): 201 packages pass, 0 fail.
- `gofmt -l .`: clean.
- `go vet ./...`, plus `go vet -tags e2e` and `GOOS=windows go vet` on the touched packages: pass.
- `GOOS=windows go build ./...` and `GOOS=linux go build ./...`: pass.
- `golangci-lint run` v2.13.2: 0 issues.

Earlier runs:
- On `9eddae46b3` (round 1, before the rebase): `go test -count=1 -tags e2e -v -run 'TestE2E_' ./internal/cli/` passed all 13 E2E tests.
- On `0ec383d438` (an earlier version of the second commit, before review), the full suite in the machine's own environment hit two environment-only failures, `opencodev2` (a locally installed OpenCode 1) and `integration` (ambient `CLAUDE_CODE_*` variables). Both pass once isolated.

RED, then GREEN. Each line names the commit the test failed on:
- Initial change, on `f9bf27a9a9` (before the rebase; now `b97ecdca73`):
  - The `datadirlock` API did not exist.
  - `ao import` opened and migrated `ao.db` while the lock was held (`err = <nil>`).
  - `ExitCode` returned 1, want 75.
- Round 1, on `efc024f738` (before the rebase; now `2c9832bfd4`):
  - A cancelled wait came back as `context canceled; waited 1m0s ..., refusing to start`.
  - The import refusal pointed at `ao stop`.
  - The e2e refusal said `waited 300ms`, not `7.9s`.
- Round 2, on `c2fdb93b8a`: the e2e refusal said `waited 7.9s`, not `18.9s`.
- The lab's base binary (`df4cabc544`) ran two daemons on one `ao.db`.

Not run locally:
- The Windows and Linux CI jobs: `windows-workspace` and the cli-e2e legs.
- The docs-site build (`npm run build --prefix frontend/src/docs`): the two `.mdx` edits are plain text in existing table rows, and disk is low for an `npm ci`.

## Not covered

- **Daemons from before this change don't take the lock.** On the first upgrade, a new daemon can't see an old one that is still draining, so this takeover can still overlap once. The run-file check still catches an old daemon that shares `AO_RUN_FILE`.
- **File systems that cannot lock files** run without the guard (see What), so two daemons can still share `ao.db` there. SQLite WAL is not supported on network file systems anyway.
- **An old daemon stuck past the wait still makes the new daemon exit 75.** The bound covers only the capped stages. If the old daemon is stuck in one of `Run`'s uncapped waits (startup reconcile, usage pipeline, pricing, lifecycle stack, report delivery, telemetry close) beyond 9T + 18 s, the new daemon still exits 75. The same applies to a wedged daemon that ignores SIGTERM. The desktop then shows "Daemon exited with code 75" with no retry, and the user has to stop the PID named in the message. Base would run both daemons on one `ao.db` in that case.
- **Two shutdown stages that look capped are not strictly bounded:**
  - Chat `StopAll` first runs `sides.stopAll()`, which closes every side conversation outside `chatStopCtx` (`service/chat/service.go:1622`, `side.go:1489`).
  - `managedPreview.Close()` gives each running preview server up to 7 s, one after another (`previewserver/manager.go:505-516`), so this stage grows with the number of preview servers.

  Either can push a predecessor past the wait.
- The desktop has no dedicated UI or auto-retry for exit 75.
- `backend/main.go` (the `go run .` compatibility wrapper) still exits 1 on a refused start.
- `sqlite.OpenReadOnly` readers, such as the dev project import from another data dir, take no lock. They never migrate.

Others: +267 -24  

Adds three editable starter templates to make automation setup discoverable and measure which starting points people choose:

title: fix(desktop): only stop an orphaned daemon whose identity is confirmed
body:
Code changes: +170 -54  
Tests: +170 -11  
Others: +0 -0

## Impact

| | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| Stale `running.json` names a live, unrelated process (3 runs) | killed 3 of 3 | **left alive 3 of 3** |
| Same, and that process leads a process group | whole group killed 3 of 3 | **all alive 3 of 3** |
| A daemon answers `/healthz`, the stale file names an unrelated PID | unrelated process killed; step 8,154 ms | daemon replaced, unrelated process alive; step **9 ms** |
| Hung real daemon (the case this step exists for) | killed; 2,009 ms | killed; 2,010 ms (unchanged) |

## What

The desktop app no longer SIGTERMs whatever process a stale `running.json` names. When it has to clear a process that is holding the daemon port, it signals only a process it can identify as the AO daemon. When it leaves a live process named by `running.json` alone, it logs why.

## Why

`running.json` outlives the daemon after a crash, a hard kill or a reboot, and the OS then gives the recorded PID to an unrelated process. At launch, once both attach paths had failed, `startDaemonInner` treated any live run-file PID (`process.kill(pid, 0)`) as "a wedged daemon holding the port" and sent SIGTERM to that PID's whole process group, then to the PID itself. With a reused PID that kills an unrelated process, or its whole group, when the app starts. The same code had two more problems:

- When a daemon did answer the probe, it still signalled the PID in the file instead of the PID the daemon reported. It killed the unrelated process and left the daemon holding the port.
- A corrupt file with `pid: -1` is truthy, passes `kill(-1, 0)`, and reaches `kill(-1, SIGTERM)`.

`ao stop` and the daemon's own stale-file check already refuse to act on a PID that `/healthz` has not confirmed. The desktop was the odd one out. There is no tracking issue for this.

## How

- `portHolderPidToReplace` (`frontend/src/shared/daemon-takeover.ts`) replaces `shouldReplacePortHolder`. It returns `{ pid }` to signal, or `{ pid: null, reason }`:
  - A probe answered: the PID the probe reported, whatever the file says.
  - Nothing answered: the run-file PID, only if that process began no later than 5 s after the run-file's `startedAt`. The daemon stamps `startedAt` after it boots, so the process that wrote the file is always older than it; a process that reused the PID started after the daemon died, so it is always younger. This keeps recovery of a hung daemon that holds the port and has stopped answering.
  - A PID of 1 or less, or a non-integer, is never returned.
- `readProcessStartMs` (`frontend/src/main/process-start.ts`) reads the start time from `ps -o etime=` (whole seconds, no locale or timezone to parse). It returns null when the process is gone, `ps` fails, or the platform is Windows, and null always means "do not signal".
- `frontend/src/main.ts`: the orphan step asks for the PID, signals it as before (process group, then the PID), and only then waits for the port and removes the run-file. With no identified holder it goes straight to spawn; the new daemon overwrites a stale run-file itself. If `running.json` names a process that is alive but is not signalled, the app logs `AO: not stopping process <pid> named by running.json: <reason>` (for example "it started 7200 s after running.json was written, so it is not the daemon that wrote it", or "its start time could not be read"), so a hung daemon that was not replaced can be diagnosed. The other `process.kill` calls either send signal 0 or signal a child this app spawned and still holds.

## Evidence

The orphan step lives inside `startDaemonInner` and cannot be imported without Electron. A harness (not part of this PR) takes `main.ts` from `origin/main` and from this branch, slices the orphan block out verbatim, and runs it with each tree's own `shared/` and `main/` modules, real `ps`, real signals to real processes, and isolated `AO_DATA_DIR` / `AO_RUN_FILE` / `AO_PORT`. Its `process.kill` only reaches processes the harness spawned. PID reuse is emulated with a run-file whose `startedAt` is older than the live process.

| Scenario | Base (`origin/main`) | This branch |
|---|---|---|
| Stale `running.json` names a live unrelated `sleep` (3 runs) | killed 3/3, run-file removed | alive 3/3, no signal, run-file left, warning logged 3/3 |
| Same, the PID is a group leader (`sh` plus a `sleep` child) (3 runs) | whole group killed 3/3 | both alive 3/3, no signal, warning logged 3/3 |
| Hung daemon: holds the port, never answers, `startedAt` after its start (3 runs) | killed 3/3, step 2009 ms (2006-2018) | killed 3/3, step 2010 ms (2009-2019) |
| A daemon answers `/healthz`, the stale file names an unrelated PID (3 runs) | unrelated process killed 3/3, daemon still answering, step 8154 ms (8018-8174) | daemon killed 3/3, unrelated process alive 3/3, step 9 ms (8-15) |
| Hung daemon, but `ps` cannot be run (the Windows situation, reproduced on macOS) (3 runs) | killed 3/3 | alive 3/3, no signal, warning logged 3/3 ("its start time could not be read ...") |
| Corrupt file, `pid: -1` (3 runs, calls recorded, none delivered) | `kill(-1, 0)`, `kill(1, SIGTERM)`, `kill(-1, SIGTERM)` | no SIGTERM; only the signal-0 liveness check, warning logged |
| Real Go daemon (lab sandbox) hung with SIGSTOP, file written by the daemon (1 run each) | SIGTERM delivered, clean shutdown | SIGTERM delivered, clean shutdown |

The hung-daemon step is dominated by the 2 s probe timeout; the added `ps` read is about 1 ms. For the real daemon, `startedAt` minus the process start read by `readProcessStartMs` was +693 to +3127 ms over ten readings in two runs (the rule needs at least -5000). Measured on a MacBook Pro (Apple M3 Pro), macOS 26.5.1, Node v26.8.1. Branch runs are on `117d9ab024`; base runs are on `origin/main`, whose orphan block is unchanged through `7dceb0ec7d`.

## Testing

- On `117d9ab024`: `cd frontend && npx vitest run src/shared/daemon-takeover.test.ts src/main/process-start.test.ts`: 2 files, 41 tests passed. They were written first and failed before the change.
- On `117d9ab024`: `npx vitest run src/shared src/main`: 84 files, 1587 passed, 1 skipped.
- On `117d9ab024`: `npm run typecheck` and `npm run typecheck:e2e`: no errors.
- Full `npx vitest run`, made on the first commit before the rebase (`7833584b3a` on `9ba118107b`): 474 of 476 files passed. Three tests failed while the machine was under heavy load (load average up to 49): two in `CreateProjectFlow.test.tsx` and a 20 s timeout in `browser-history-store.test.ts`. All 84 tests in those two files pass when run alone, and none of them imports a changed module. The second commit changes only the modules and tests covered by the runs above, plus the orphan step in `main.ts`, which no test imports.
- The `ps -o etime=` output format and exit code were also checked against procps-ng 4.0.2 in a Linux container.
- Not run: the Playwright renderer smoke job, the guarded-navigation browser integration (needs the pinned agent-browser download), the docs build, the macOS Swift helper job, the cloud-client and product-ui package checks, and anything Go (no backend file changed).

## Not covered

- **Windows has no start-time reader**, so `readProcessStartMs` returns null there and a hung daemon that has stopped answering is no longer force-killed. That is not harmless. A new daemon does not exit on a busy port: it falls back to an ephemeral one (`backend/internal/httpd/server.go`), and the only guard against a second daemon is the old one answering `/healthz` with the PID in `running.json` (`backend/internal/daemon/daemon.go`). A hung daemon answers nothing, so on Windows the replacement daemon now starts beside it on the same data dir (or contends for a database lock the hung one holds). `ao stop` refuses an unresponsive daemon (`backend/internal/cli/stop.go`), so the user would need Task Manager or `taskkill`. The only trace is the log line above; nothing is shown in the UI. A daemon that still answers the probe is replaced as before, and the Windows PID-reuse hazard itself is closed. The evidence row "`ps` cannot be run" reproduces the consequence on macOS; nothing was run on Windows.
  - Follow-up: a Windows process start-time reader through PowerShell `Get-Process`, which needs a Windows host to verify.
  - #6799 makes a second daemon wait for and refuse a held data dir. Once both land, that closes the two-writers part of this.
- Linux was not run locally beyond the `ps` format check; CI runs the unit tests there, including the one that reads the start time of a real `sleep`.
- Real PID reuse was not provoked, and Electron itself was not launched. The kill, wait and run-file steps in `main.ts`, and the new warning, have no unit test because they need Electron; they ran through the harness above.

title: feat(harness): accounts live on the agent's page
body:
Code changes: +374 -264
Tests: +305 -168
Others: +26 -23

Stacked on #6274 (Account Manager). Review that one first; this PR changes the Settings UI on top of it, plus one field the account helper reports.

## Summary

Settings now has one page for agents and their accounts, instead of Harness and Accounts side by side. It follows "option 2" from the layout review: the agent is one line at the top, the account is everything below it.

- **Accounts nested under their agent.** Claude Code and Codex list their accounts under them in the agent list, each with Default / In reserve and what it has left, plus a "New … account" row. Opening the agent shows its default account; another account is one click.
- **The agent in one line.** Under the agent's name: status, version, install method, "vX available", and the one action that matters now (Install or Update; progress while one runs). **Details** opens a side sheet with the agent's installation and health, everything the Account and Health tabs showed before.
- **Account, Usage, Models.** The open account has three tabs, and the tab stays when another account is picked, so accounts compare quickly.
  - Account: the session rules, sign-in, rename, and the plan. The plan's models open Models; an icon on the running sessions row opens Usage.
  - Usage, in one column:
    - **Limits**, moved from Account. Each has a tick where a steady pace would leave it by now, and says "Lasts until reset" or "Behind pace". Resets, the paused row, extra usage and credits come with them.
    - **Facts:** today and 7 days of tokens, requests in 3 hours with refusals, time to first word.
    - The **last failure**, a **14-day strip**, the **sessions** on the account, the **share by model**, and the provider's own count (Codex).
    - **States:** loading keeps the limits' size, limits not reported offer Try now, and an account nothing passed through says so.
  - Models: the account's own catalogue, with efforts as small chips, under the agent-wide defaults and the enabled-model switches from #5848.
- **Details sheet.** A light scrim with no blur, eased open and close, and a grey edge.
- **Agents without accounts in AO** (every other agent, and Claude Code or Codex until an account is added): the same line and Details, then Account (the agent's own login) and Models.
- **The Accounts section is gone.** "Manage accounts" in account menus, the new-task sign-in prompt and the composer's login shortcut open the agent's page instead, focused on the right agent.

## Notes for review

- `ProviderAccountsSection.tsx` keeps its state hook and sign-in flow; it now exports the pieces the agent page nests (`AgentAccountRows`, `AgentAccountPane`) instead of a page of its own.
- `AccountDetail` takes the tab and the Models content from its caller, so the account pane does not import the harness code.
- `HarnessAccountTab` renders either its installation part (in Details) or its login part (the Account tab).
- `HarnessModelsPanel` takes a catalogue scope, so the Models tab lists one account's models.
- The account helper now reports `countingSince`, when it began counting requests, failures and first words. Those figures live in its memory, so after a restart the tab says "Since 09:12" under them instead of showing a misleading zero. Making them durable, pricing, "Runs out in …" and an expanded usage view are a separate PR.
- The estimated cost of an account's sessions leaves the tab until that PR: for sessions through the helper it was empty or partial.
- The navigation label is still "Harness"; renaming it to "Agents" touches every language and is left for a follow-up.

## Validation

- Vitest on every touched test file passes (HarnessSettingsSection, its remote variant, ProviderAccountsSection, TaskComposer, SettingsDialog, ui-store, SessionProviderAccountMenuItem), including the Models and Usage shortcuts.
- Go: `go build ./...` in backend and proxy-host; the proxy-host activity and account-state tests.
- Updating the tests found three product bugs, fixed here: clicking an account under an agent that was not open showed the default account instead; "Manage accounts" from a session waiting for a sign-in did not focus its agent; the agent's line offered Update while a login was still finishing.
- Not run locally: the frontend type-check and the full test suite; CI runs both.
- Running in the dev desktop app; not yet reviewed there.

title: perf(preview): avoid loading session history on every poll
body:
Code changes: +41 -13  
Tests: +155 -2  
Others: +42 -0 (generated sqlc)

The preview poller reads and decodes every historical session every 250 ms, then discards terminated and nonworker sessions. Large prompts and checkpoints make this recurring read expensive on long-lived hosts, even when few previews are active.

Read only session ID, workspace path, preview URL, and preview revision for nonterminated workers through a dedicated SQLite projection. Keep blank previews in the result so a deleted preview file can still be restored when it reappears. Polling cadence, explicit preview selection, and service writes stay unchanged.

Regression tests cover active/terminated/nonworker filtering, standalone workers, blank and external previews, cancellation, and forgetting terminated previews. A synthetic benchmark with 1,000 workers (990 terminated, 4 KiB prompts) measured a median read time of 8.83 ms → 0.163 ms and allocations of 10,590,888 → 4,232 bytes per read across three runs.

This was found during mobile/Cloudflare disconnect triage. It removes confirmed avoidable daemon work; whether that work contributes to the observed connection drops still requires live validation. No network, tunnel, authentication, or reconnect behavior changes are included.

Validation with Go 1.27.1 (concurrency limited locally):
- Full backend race coverage on macOS and Ubuntu; SQLite uses the four CI shards on Linux, and permission-sensitive suites were rerun successfully as an unprivileged user.
- Focused preview/store tests and full race tests for both changed packages.
- Backend build and vet; golangci-lint v2.13.2 (zero issues).
- Native macOS and Linux CLI E2E; fresh-install Docker smoke check.
- Full Cloud build/vet/race suite and the Expat build target.
- Pinned sqlc and API regeneration with no drift; gitleaks v7.4.0 scanned the one introduced commit with no leaks.

All 21 GitHub checks passed for this commit, including native Windows CLI/workspace checks and amd64 Linux race coverage ([Go](https://github.com/OrchestratorInc/agent-orchestrator/actions/runs/38834322030), [CLI E2E](https://github.com/OrchestratorInc/agent-orchestrator/actions/runs/38834322040)). Local Windows execution was unavailable; local Linux containers used arm64.

title: perf(storage): stop scanning the provider archive at every completed turn
body:
Code changes: +15 -0  
Tests: +177 -0  
Others: +0 -0

## Impact

| | before | after | change |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| `SelectVerifiedAuthenticationTurn` on a real 3.88 GB database, first run | 3.95 s | 12 ms | **-99.7%** |
| Same, warm | 281 ms | under 1 ms | -99% |
| Longest writer stall inside a turn (166k-row conversation) | 250 ms | 71 ms | -72% |
| Writer stalls of 100 ms or more, over 801 turns | 390 | 2 | -99% |
| Cost: first start after the upgrade (one-time index build) | 1.28 s | 28.9 s | once |

## What

Adds migration `20261022144835405_provider_events_turn_completed_index.sql`: a partial index on
`conversation_provider_events(branch_id, id) WHERE method = 'turn.completed'`. No query, API or UI changes; the
planner picks the index for the existing statement.

## Why

`SelectVerifiedAuthenticationTurn` decides whether a completed turn proves usable authentication. It runs:

- inside the projection write transaction of every successfully completed turn (`ReconcileConversationAuthentication`
  from the chat controller), with the turn's provider id;
- from `chat.Service.Start` with empty ids, under the writer lock, for a conversation that already has account facts:
  one lookup per completed turn of the conversation;
- on conversation reads while a re-auth demand is pending (same empty-id form).

Its `EXISTS` looked for the matching `turn.completed` archive row through `idx_conversation_provider_events_branch
(branch_id=?)`, which reads every archive row of the branch to test `method`. The archive is mostly streamed deltas,
so on a long conversation each call walked hundreds of thousands of rows while holding the single SQLite writer.
There is no tracking issue. An earlier analysis (2026-10-14, not part of this PR's measurements) of a real long-lived
database with a 191k-row conversation measured 2.4 s cold and 0.15 s warm per call, and 3 ms and under 1 ms with a
partial index. This PR's own measurements are under Evidence.

## How

- `20261022144835405_provider_events_turn_completed_index.sql` creates `idx_conversation_provider_events_turn_completed`. Only
  `turn.completed` rows get an entry, so the index holds one row per completed turn and no other archive insert pays
  for it. `Down` drops it.
- No query change: `EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN` for the `EXISTS` goes from
  `SEARCH e USING INDEX idx_conversation_provider_events_branch (branch_id=?)` to
  `SEARCH e USING INDEX idx_conversation_provider_events_turn_completed (branch_id=?)`. The planner picks it with and
  without statistics (checked on the real-size clone before and after a full `ANALYZE`).
- The first start after upgrade builds the index inside `sqlite.Open`, before the daemon reports ready: 28.9 s against
  1.28 s on a 3.9 GB clone, and it grows with the size of the archive table (cost under Evidence).
- Ledger entry in `migrate_burned_versions_test.go`.
- Migration ID: `20261022144835405`, a UTC timestamp ID in the format `npm run migration:create` generates. Main switched from sequential numbers to timestamp IDs after this branch was cut, and its `0200` is now `0200_session_artifact_version_source.sql`.

## Evidence

Measured three ways; counts, sizes and timings only. The machine was shared and busy: the 1-minute load average
recorded with each measurement was 8 to 20 for the real-clone runs, 10 to 32 for the end-to-end runs and 18 to 133 for
the synthetic ones, so wall times are upper bounds and CPU time is shown where it matters. "Cold" is the first run on a
fresh `cp -c` clone, "warm" a re-run in the same session. Apple M3 Pro, macOS 26.5.1, Go 1.27.1, SQLite 3.51.0 (CLI)
and 3.53.3 (Go driver).

**1. Real data, production statement.** A clone of a real long-lived database (3.88 GB, schema 194, 2.29M archive rows;
the live file was held open by the desktop daemon, so this is the offline backup of 2026-10-11 that the perf lab clones).
Its conversation with the most archive rows has 191,418 on its active branch and 3 completed turns. The statement is the
sqlc text with its parameters bound; "before" is the clone as it stands, "after" a second clone with the migration's
`CREATE INDEX` run in the sqlite3 CLI. 5 clones per state, median; these are this PR's numbers, taken on a busier
machine than the earlier analysis's 2.4 s / 0.15 s:

| | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| statement, first run: wall (CPU) | 3.95 s (0.70 s) | 12 ms (3.7 ms) |
| statement, warm: wall (CPU) | 281 ms (226 ms) | under 1 ms (0.10 ms) |
| empty-id form (chat start), first run / warm, wall | 3.55 s / 228 ms | 12 ms / under 1 ms |
| first start on a clone, daemon spawn to ready (lab, 3 runs per binary) | 1.28 s | 28.9 s (28.9 to 29.9) |

**2. End to end.** Perf lab: real daemon, scripted ACP agent, one conversation grown to 166,401 archive rows and 800
completed turns, then one more short turn; binary built from the merge-base against this branch, 3 repetitions each,
alternating, every measured turn completed, no comparability warning. A probe beside the daemon records stretches of 10 ms
or more in which it could not take the writer. Median (range):

| | base | branch |
|---|---|---|
| turn time as the lab sees it (20 ms polling) | 0.497 s (0.447 to 0.539) | 0.346 s (0.315 to 0.609) |
| daemon CPU during the turn | 0.464 s (0.424 to 0.528) | 0.272 s (0.263 to 0.500) |
| longest stretch the writer was unavailable inside the turn | 250 ms (245 to 267) | 71 ms (60 to 102) |
| stretches of 100 ms or more over the run's 801 turn completions | 390 (382 to 458) | 2 (2 to 7) |
| total time in stretches of 50 ms or more over the run | 78.5 s (74.4 to 99.1) | 1.8 s (0.5 to 3.2) |

The archive fits in the page cache here, so the extra work in the base is the 0.19 s of daemon CPU shown (0.464 s vs
0.272 s); the real clone above shows what the scan costs when the archive does not fit.

**3. More completed turns.** After the index the lookup walks one entry per completed turn, and the real conversation
has 3. A synthetic 3.3 GB database (2.3M archive rows, one conversation with 191,000 of them) with 500 and with 50
completed turns shows the other end. The turn-completion transaction (archive insert, settle, reconcile; the production
`ProjectProviderEvent` path, timed whole, which is how long the writer is held), cold / warm, median of 5:

| completed turns | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| 500 | 1.93 s / 291 ms | 155 ms / 5.1 ms |
| 50 | 1.62 s / 178 ms | 19 ms / 1.3 ms |

The empty-id form runs the lookup once per completed turn: at 500 turns it went from 32 s of CPU (wall 60 to 94 s) to
0.16 s; at 50 turns from 3.7 s to 7.5 ms.

**Cost.** Writes: 200,000 `reasoning.delta` inserts cost 2.02 s of CPU before and 1.96 s after (50,000 through the
`branch_id` trigger: 0.80 s and 0.71 s); only `turn.completed` rows get an entry. One-time index build: one scan of the
2,740 MiB archive table on the real-size clone, 4.1 s of CPU; 41 s of wall for the bare statement on a cold clone, 28.9 s
inside a daemon start (table above). The index is small: 31 pages (124 KiB) for 2,242 entries on that clone, taken from
its free pages, so the file did not grow.

Method: every measurement here ran with the branch at `24adc9cfc2` against its then merge-base `9ba118107b` (the SQL of the
migration is the same on the final head). The statement text comes from the generated sqlc code. "Before" is the same database without the index. "After"
is, on the real clone, the migration's `CREATE INDEX` run in the sqlite3 CLI (the daemon-start row runs the real
migration in the branch daemon), and, on the synthetic database, the database after the real migration through
`sqlite.Open`. The transaction timings call the production `Store` methods from a scratch test binary that is not part
of the repository.

## Testing

title: fix(mobile): make the mux session subscription match the daemon protocol
body:
Code changes: +24 -14  
Tests: +292 -6  
Others: +0 -0

## Impact

| During one streaming turn | before | after |
|---|---:|---:|
| Session-update frames a subscribed mobile client receives | 0 | **2,008** |
| Of those, delivered with data that matches `change_log` | 0 | **2,008 of 2,008** |

No screen subscribes yet, so nothing changes for users until one does.

## What

No app code calls `subscribeSessions()` today, so this changes nothing a phone user can see yet. It makes the mobile mux session subscription match the daemon protocol on both sides, so the first screen that uses it works. Two mismatches are fixed:

1. **Send.** The subscribe frame had no `type`. The daemon requires `type: "subscribe"` and dropped the frame without an error, so a subscribed phone never got an event.
2. **Receive.** The daemon pushes one change per frame as `session: {seq, projectId, sessionId, eventType}`. `MuxClient` read `sessions`, a list of `SessionPatch`, so `onSessions` ran for every frame with an empty list. `onSessions` and `SessionPatch` are replaced by `onSessionUpdate` and `SessionUpdate`. Nothing used the old names.

The daemon is unchanged.

## Why

**Send.** The daemon routes on `ch` and then on `type`, and `handleSubscribe` (`backend/internal/terminal/manager.go`) returns unless `type` is `"subscribe"`. `MuxClient` sent `{ch:"subscribe", topics:[...]}` from two copies of the literal, and nothing reported the drop. [ADR 0004](docs/adr/0004-cloudflare-tunnel-for-remote-mobile-access.md) names this subscription (`{ch: "subscribe", topics: [...]}`) as the existing hook for moving conversation events onto the mux, so whoever builds that needs it to work. I found no existing issue for this.

**Receive.** The `ch:"sessions"` payload is one `change_log` row, not session state (`sessionUpdate` in `backend/internal/terminal/protocol.go`; the client refetches detail over REST). `sessionId` is omitted for a project-level change. `SessionPatch` needs `status`, `activity`, `attentionLevel` and `lastActivityAt`, which are not on the wire, so the callback is reshaped rather than adapted. Measured with only the send fix applied: `onSessions` ran 2,008 times in one streaming turn and every call got an empty list.

**Frames checked.** Only these two frame types were wrong. `exited` also reads a `code` the daemon never sends (see Not covered).

| Direction | Frame | Mobile | Daemon | Match |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| to daemon | subscribe | `{ch:"subscribe", topics}` | needs `type:"subscribe"` | no, fixed |
| to daemon | terminal open | `{ch:"terminal", id, type:"open", projectId, role:"secondary"}` | reads `ch`, `id`, `type`, `role`; `projectId` is ignored | yes |
| to daemon | terminal data, resize, close | `type`, `id`, base64 `data`, `cols`, `rows` | same fields | yes |
| to daemon | system ping | `{ch:"system", type:"ping"}` | answers `pong` | yes (pong received live) |
| to phone | sessions change | read `sessions` | sends `session` | no, fixed |
| to phone | terminal opened, data, error, resize | handled by `type` | same names and fields | yes (the terminal screen depends on them) |
| to phone | terminal exited | `onTerminalExited(id, msg.code ?? 0)` | sends `ch`, `id`, `type` only | frame yes, `code` no: always 0 (not fixed here) |

The desktop renderer (`terminal-mux.ts`) is the only other `/mux` client. Every frame it sends carries `type`, and it sends no subscribe frame (it gets events over SSE).

**The daemon does not accept the old type-less frame.** No shipped build sent it: `subscribeSessions()` has no caller in the app code (only its definition and this PR's tests use it), the reconnect path only sends the frame after that method ran, and the history from before the repository's import shows no caller either. The daemon's `type` check predates the mobile mux client (the check is from early June 2026, the client from early July 2026, both before the history import), so the typed frame works against every daemon it can meet. Accepting the old frame would heal no client and would loosen the one check every other channel obeys. `TestMuxSubscribeFrame/frame_without_type_is_ignored` pins the choice.

## How

- `packages/mobile/lib/mux.ts`: one `SUBSCRIBE_FRAME` constant with `type`, shared by `subscribeSessions()` and the reconnect path. `SessionUpdate` and `onSessionUpdate(update)` replace `SessionPatch` and `onSessions`; `handle` reads `session`, requires a numeric `seq` and string `projectId` and `eventType`, passes `sessionId` when present, and drops a `sessions` frame that lacks them. The class comment no longer calls the frames status snapshots.
- `packages/mobile/lib/mux.test.ts`: drives `MuxClient` with a fake `WebSocket` and fake timers set up once in an outer `describe`. It pins every frame the client sends as literal JSON (including the subscribe frame after a reconnect) and feeds it the daemon's two golden session frames.
- `backend/internal/terminal/protocol_test.go`: decodes the client literals with the daemon's `clientMsg`, and adds the golden for a project-level change (no `sessionId`), so both received literals come from the daemon's own marshalling. The existing `fakeConn` tests pass ready-made structs, so they could not see a frame that decodes to something else.
- `backend/internal/httpd/terminal_mux_test.go`: sends the subscribe frame as raw text over a real websocket and counts the session frames for one CDC event: 1 for the typed frame, 0 for the type-less one. A ping/pong round trip orders the check, so there is no sleep.

## Evidence

Real `MuxClient` code (the merge-base, first-commit and final copies of `mux.ts`) against an isolated perf-lab daemon built from the merge-base, during one `text` streaming turn (2,000 chunks at 200/s). Four clients were connected to the same turn. Ground truth is the `change_log` rows the daemon wrote in the turn. The after client is asserted, not just counted: every frame must parse into an update with non-empty session data that matches the `change_log` row with the same `seq`.

| | Before (merge-base) | Step 1 (typed frame, old handler) | After (final) | Control (final, never subscribes) |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| `ch:"sessions"` frames received in the turn, median (min-max of 3) | 0 (0-0) | 2,008 (2,008-2,008) | 2,008 (2,008-2,008) | 0 (0-0) |
| Handler calls with non-empty session data | 0 | 0 | 2,008 | 0 |
| Of those, matching their `change_log` row | n/a | n/a | 2,008 | 0 |
| `change_log` rows written in the turn | 2,008 | 2,008 | 2,008 | 2,008 |

All 3 turns completed and all assertions held. Step 1 shows the receive-side bug on its own: frames arrive, and the old handler runs 2,008 times without data. The after client lost nothing (0 missing, 0 duplicates). Every client received a pong to its own ping, so the zeros are not a dead socket. The control is what the app does today. The run used `cc4b0b2dca` and `2b4cd29daf`; the later commit `d688b785fc` changes only test code and a test comment (`mux.ts` is byte-identical). Method, commands, environment and raw data: `evidence.md` and `mux-subscribe-ab-text.json` (kept outside the repo).

## Testing

The branch has three commits: `cc4b0b2dca` (send side), `2b4cd29daf` (receive side) and `d688b785fc` (shared test setup; the final head).

- **Send side, on `cc4b0b2dca`.** RED: `cd packages/mobile && npx vitest run lib/mux.test.ts` on the unfixed `mux.ts`: 3 failed (the diff shows the missing `"type": "subscribe"`), 15 passed. GREEN: 18 passed.
- **Receive side, on `2b4cd29daf`.** RED: with the old handler the three new session-frame tests fail (`expected [] to deeply equal [[{seq: 7, ...}]]`: the callback never ran for the daemon's frame); the fourth, which checks that unreadable frames are dropped, passes before and after. GREEN: 22 passed.
- **Daemon mutation checks** (the daemon is unchanged, so the server tests pass before and after; each break was reverted): accepting a type-less frame fails `frame_without_type_is_ignored`; a different subscribe type fails `typed_frame_subscribes` and the decode test; a daemon that sends an empty `sessionId` fails the project-level golden.
- **Final head `d688b785fc`, mobile.** `cd packages/mobile && npm run typecheck && npm test` on Node 20.20.2 (the CI major): clean; 214 files and 1,915 tests pass. Against the unfixed `mux.ts` the restructured tests give 6 failed, 16 passed.
- **Final head `d688b785fc`, backend.** `cd backend`: `gofmt -l .` clean; `go build ./...`; `go vet ./...`; `golangci-lint run` (v2.13.2): 0 issues; `go test -race -count=1 ./internal/terminal/... ./internal/httpd/...` passes.
- **Final head `d688b785fc`, full suite.** `go test -p 4 -count=1 ./...` (no `-race`): 197 packages pass, 4 fail. Three fail the same way on the unchanged merge-base `5418c4631b` in 3 of 3 re-runs: `opencodev2` `TestV2RejectsFailuresWithoutSideEffects` (reads the developer's installed OpenCode 1.19.0), `integration` `TestClaudeResumeHookConfirmsNativeIdentityForCurrentLaunch`, and `conpty` `TestDarwinPTYCloseDoesNotWaitOutAShellThatIgnoresSIGTERM` (a 500 ms grace). The fourth, `tmux` (`TestRuntimeIntegrationLegacyDefaultSocketDestroyEnforcesDetachOnDestroy` and `TestRuntimeIntegrationSupervisedExitKeepsInteractiveShell`), failed only under the full-suite load and passes 3 of 3 alone on both the merge-base and the branch.
- **All three commits, secrets.** `gitleaks` 8.30.0 over `origin/main..HEAD`: no leaks, with its default rules and with the repo's rules (`.github/.gitleaks.toml`, converted for gitleaks 8: an `id` per rule, allowlist `files` as `paths`; a planted fake token is caught by the converted rules). CI pins gitleaks 7.4.0 with the unconverted file, which I could not run (Linux binary).
- **Not run locally; verify in CI:** `windows-workspace` (Windows runner), `cloud-build-test`, `chat-race`, `session-store-race`, `sqlite-race` (no change in their packages; `cloud-build-test` also has a Docker step), `cli-e2e` (starts daemons outside the lab sandbox; no non-test Go file changed), `sqlc-drift`, `api-drift` (no query or API change).

## Not covered

- The daemon ignores `topics` and sends every change of every project to every subscribed client: about 196 frames/s, about 25 KB/s, during one streaming turn. [ADR 0004](docs/adr/0004-cloudflare-tunnel-for-remote-mobile-access.md) says the mux "already has a topic subscription"; the subscription exists, the topics do not. Not edited here. A consumer should plan for this volume before it subscribes a phone on a metered link.
- What the phone does with an update (which screen subscribes, how it refetches over REST, any debounce) is not decided, because no consumer exists.
- `exited` carries no exit code. The daemon sends `{ch, id, type:"exited"}` (`manager.go`; `serverMsg` has no code field, and `terminal-mux.ts` documents `exited{id}`), but `MuxClient` reads `msg.code ?? 0`. So `onTerminalExited` always gets 0, and `terminalExitedCopy`'s "ended unexpectedly" banner for a non-zero code can never show. Not fixed here: it needs the daemon to report a code, or the copy to stop depending on one.
- The terminal `open` frame was not driven against a live daemon (the lab sandbox has no PTY runtime). It is covered by the decode test and the existing `TestMuxUpgradeStreamsTerminal`.
- Only the `text` scenario, on loopback, with Node's `WebSocket` instead of React Native's.

title: perf(chat): batch streamed text deltas into one SQLite write per flush
body:
Code changes: +365 -85  
Tests: +1177 -0  
Others: +7 -2  

## Impact

| | before | after | change |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Daemon disk written, `text` turn (2,000 chunks) | 168.5 MB | 25.6 MB | **-85%** |
| Same, `reasoning` turn | 137.4 MB | 25.7 MB | **-81%** |
| Same, `realistic` turn (reasoning + two tools) | 300.2 MB | 194.1 MB | -35% |
| `change_log` rows, `text` turn | 2,008 | 208 | -90% |
| Daemon CPU, `text` turn | 2.05 s | 1.19 s | -42% |
| Replay of 20,544 deltas after a daemon restart | 9.51 s | 3.73 s | -61% |

Trade-off: the API shows streamed text growing 20 times a second (gaps of 70 ms at most) instead of at every poll. Turn wall time is unchanged (10.0 s).

## What

The Chat projector now writes streamed deltas in runs. Consecutive deltas of one stream (message text, reasoning, command output, terminal input, tool progress for the same provider item) are committed in one SQLite transaction instead of one transaction per token. Apart from the intentional changes listed below, the transcript is the same: same final text, same timeline rows and sequences, same caps and truncation flags, same CDC row types, same archive order.

This is a narrower alternative to the batching half of #5176: durable batching only, no live preview stream, no new endpoints, no frontend changes, and it covers deltas that carry native event ids (the persistent Claude ACP path), which #5176 skipped.

## Why

Every provider event was its own archive+projection transaction behind the store's single writer. A 20-character token costs an archive insert, the archive `branch_id` trigger update, a `text || ?` rewrite of the whole message or activity row, a revision bump and a `change_log` row. On a fresh DB, one 2,000-chunk reply made the daemon write 168.5 MB to disk on `df4cabc544` (median of 3), about 18.5 WAL frames per chunk (earlier lab WAL trace). On slow or network storage this is what makes replies crawl: #4657 reports first prompts taking more than three minutes with the data dir on NFS. This implements CH-2 in `docs/plans/2026-10-13-desktop-performance-overhaul.md`.

Relates to #4657. Alternative to the batching part of #5176.

## How

- **Pump** (`delta_batch.go`): `Controller.project()` hands the provider channel to `pumpProviderEvents`, which hands the old per-event loop body (now `projectUnit`) one unit at a time: a single event, or a run of deltas that are identical except for their text and native event id. Reading stays on the projector goroutine, so while a write runs, events wait in the adapter's bounded channel as before; Codex and ACP backpressure and drop rules are unchanged.
- **When a run is written**: before any other event (item/turn completion, approvals, errors, controller state), when the stream ends (shutdown, detach, provider exit), when Stop asks for it, at 32 KiB or 1,024 events, and no later than 50 ms after its first delta. Once nothing more is queued, a run is written at once if it starts a different stream from the last run written, or if no run was written in the last 50 ms. So an idle writer adds no latency, and a new item's first delta, which creates its row and takes its timeline position, is not held back. While one stream keeps going it costs one write per 50 ms, and deltas that queue while a write runs join the next run.
- **Archive and dedupe**: deltas without a native event id are never deduplicated, so their run is archived as one row holding the joined text. Deltas with one (persistent ACP host, Unreal Agent) keep one archive row per event inside the run's single transaction, and only text whose row was actually inserted is applied. A persistent host replays an unacknowledged prompt from its start and the replay can be cut into different runs; a run keyed by one id would either drop new deltas behind an already-archived first id or re-apply text, so per-event ids are the only key that stays exact. The nested archive calls reuse the store's existing projection-transaction context.
- **Stop**: after cancelling any running side-question or prompt-suggestion fork, `Interrupt` commits its pending run before taking the dispatch lock. Late deltas can still arrive during or after cancellation: SQLite appends their text while keeping messages on terminal turns settled, including a first-seen late message. No extra flush or controller lock is needed.
- **Caps**: `substr(old || delta, 1, cap)` preserves caps and truncation for joined deltas without NUL. A NUL-bearing delta is a singleton boundary: SQLite stops that append at NUL, while subsequent chunks remain separate and retain the original text and truncation behavior.
- **Empty `message.completed`**: settling a message with empty text now keeps the streamed text instead of erasing it (see "Intentional behaviour changes"). One-line store change; no query change.

### Intentional behaviour changes

- An empty `message.completed` no longer erases the streamed reply; it only stops the streaming marker. This follows `ChatEvent.Text` ("Empty means the provider settled nothing") and matches what the activity path already does for an empty settle.
- On a provider without a persistent host (no replay), a write that fails now loses the whole run (up to 32 KiB or 1,024 deltas of one stream) instead of a single delta. A message's and a reasoning item's settle event restores their text; command output and terminal input have no settled restatement. Persistent hosts are unaffected: an unacknowledged run is replayed.
- Revision counters (and the `change_log` rows their triggers emit) advance once per write instead of once per token. Clients treat revision as an opaque version.

## Evidence

Measured in an isolated lab: a real AO daemon on a fresh scratch DB, sandboxed, driving a **Claude Chat session whose scripted ACP agent runs under the persistent `ao chat-host`**. That is the #4657 path: every chunk carries a native event id, so on this path the branch still writes one archive row per chunk (archive rows and bytes are unchanged by design). The savings come from writing each run in one transaction: one row rewrite, one revision bump and one `change_log` row per run instead of per chunk. The table was measured before the branch was rebased: base `df4cabc544` (its merge-base then) vs branch `9d52aacc47` (the same two commits before the rebase). Each scenario ran 3 times per build, back to back. Every turn completed, and the lab's comparability check (scenario, parameters, DB mode, script hashes) raised no warnings. Values are medians of 3.

| Scenario | daemon disk written (physical) | daemon writes (logical) | daemon CPU | `change_log` rows | message + activity revisions | archive rows | turn wall |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| `text`: 2,000 chunks of 20 chars at 200/s | 168.5 → 25.6 MB (0.15x) | 161.6 → 27.5 MB | 2.05 → 1.19 s | 2,008 → 208 | 2,000 → 200 | 2,006 → 2,006 | 10.0 → 10.0 s |
| `reasoning`: 1,500 thought + 500 message chunks | 137.4 → 25.7 MB (0.19x) | 134.6 → 25.2 MB | 2.02 → 1.28 s | 2,011 → 211 | 2,002 → 202 | 2,008 → 2,008 | 10.0 → 10.0 s |
| `realistic`: reasoning + a shell tool (256 KB) + an edit tool (200 KB) | 300.2 → 194.1 MB (0.65x) | 289.7 → 190.4 MB | 4.44 → 2.86 s | 2,218 → 415 | 2,205 → 402 | 2,216 → 2,216 | 11.0 → 11.0 s |

- Turn wall time is unchanged because the agent paces chunks at 200/s on a local SSD; the latency problem in #4657 needs slow storage, which the lab does not emulate.
- In `realistic`, most of the remaining bytes are tool snapshots (203 `activity.started` updates carrying accumulated tool content). Those are not deltas, so this change leaves them alone.
- Nothing is deferred past the turn: a 3 s tail window after each turn showed 0 bytes written and 0 rows on both builds.
- The unchanged `ao chat-host` process used +0.05 s / +0.13 s / -0.15 s CPU on the branch across the three scenarios; not investigated, and small next to the daemon's saving.
- The WAL file's size at turn end was larger in `realistic` (7.4 vs 4.7 MB; same in the other two). That is the file's high-water size, not bytes written: fewer, larger commits give the 1,000-page auto-checkpoint fewer chances to restart the log.

**After the rebase onto `5418c4631b`** (upstream changed the chat controller's send/retry path and added a `continuation` column to message inserts; the project loop, delta update queries, `ProjectProviderEvent` and `Interrupt` are unchanged), `text` was re-run with base = the new merge-base `5418c4631b` and branch = the rebased head `b3434c1c08`, 3 runs each, all completed, no comparability warnings: daemon disk written 167.3 → 25.6 MB (0.15x), logical 161.3 → 27.5 MB, `change_log` rows 2,008 → 208, message revisions 2,000 → 200, archive rows 2,006 → 2,006, turn wall 10.0 → 10.0 s, daemon CPU 3.37 → 1.23 s (CPU varies most on this shared machine).

**Streaming still reaches the API incrementally** (measured before the rebase, `df4cabc544` vs `9d52aacc47`). The conversation endpoint was polled every ~10 ms during the `text` and `reasoning` turns, 2 runs per build:

| Stream | build | visible updates per s | median gap | max gap | polls in streaming window |
|---|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| `text` reply | base | 62.8 / 65.9 | 15 ms / 15 ms | 147 ms / 38 ms | 630 / 660 |
| `text` reply | branch | 19.9 / 19.9 | 48 ms / 48 ms | 68 ms / 70 ms | 644 / 648 |
| `reasoning`: thoughts, then reply | base | 58.3 / 59.8 | 17 ms / 15 ms | 42 ms / 141 ms | 582 / 598 |
| `reasoning`: thoughts, then reply | branch | 20.0 / 20.0 | 47 ms / 48 ms | 67 ms / 70 ms | 658 / 658 |

Two runs per build (run 1 / run 2). The poller asks every ~10 ms and a request takes a few ms, so base's rate (~60/s, a new length at almost every poll) is limited by the poll cycle, not by the stream. The branch shows the text growing 20 times a second, never more than 70 ms apart, which is the 50 ms write window. Lengths only; the final lengths matched on both builds (40,000 reply chars in `text`; 19,500 reasoning + 10,000 reply chars in `reasoning`).

**Replay through a real persistent host** (`TestACPReplayProjectsExactlyOnceAcrossDaemonRestarts`: 20,544 identified deltas replayed into real SQLite after a daemon restart; non-race test binaries, run alternately): base `5418c4631b` 9.51 s / 11.08 s vs branch `b3434c1c08` 3.73 s / 3.60 s on the final head (and before the rebase, `df4cabc544` 8.78 s / 8.65 s vs `a4b15c4de8` 3.67 s / 3.56 s), with the same exactly-once assertions.

**Write transactions** (controller test, real store, 520 queued deltas over four streams including both caps; run on `b3434c1c08`): 520 → 8, for deltas with and without native ids, with an identical persisted transcript and archive.

How it was measured: each run starts its own `ao daemon` with an isolated `AO_DATA_DIR`, `AO_RUN_FILE` and port inside a sandbox, creates a Claude Chat session, waits for the daemon to go quiet, then sends the scenario prompt. Disk bytes and CPU come from the daemon's own `proc_pid_rusage` counters (physical `ri_diskio_byteswritten`, logical `ri_logical_writes`, user + system time), sampled just before the prompt and at turn end. Row counts come from read-only DB marks taken at the same points. Environment: Mac15,6 (M3 Pro), macOS 26.5.1, Go 1.27.1, Low Power Mode on, AC power, on a machine shared with other work (a lock keeps lab measurements from overlapping).

## Testing (original batching implementation)

The commands below ran on the rebased batching head `b3434c1c08` (merge-base `5418c4631b`), with Go 1.27.1:

- `go test -race -count=1 -timeout=20m -run "^(<shard>)$" ./internal/service/chat` for both CI shards (532 tests) on `b3434c1c08`: pass (447.6 s and 356.0 s).
- `go test -race -count=1 -timeout=20m ./internal/session_manager ./internal/storage/sqlite/store` on `b3434c1c08`: pass.
- `go test -count=1 -v -run '<the new batching tests, the ACP replay test, the persistent-ack test>' ./internal/service/chat/` on `b3434c1c08`: pass.

title: fix(storage): refuse to open a database migrated by a newer AO
body:
Code changes: +116 -3  
Tests: +487 -0  
Others: +2 -0

## Impact

| | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| Start on a database a newer AO already migrated | starts against a schema it does not know; nothing logged | **refuses in 153 ms** with one stderr line; database untouched |
| Cost of the check on every start | none | 175 µs |

## What

`sqlite.Open` now refuses a database that a newer AO already migrated (`sqlite.ErrSchemaNewer`) instead of running this build against a schema it does not know. Both production callers, the daemon and `ao import`, report it as one line on stderr and exit 1:

```
open store: database schema is newer than this AO build: <data dir>/ao.db has migration 20261023093000123 applied, but this build only includes migrations up to 20261022172135175. A newer AO has already migrated this data directory: update AO, or point AO_DATA_DIR at a different directory. Developers switching branches can set AO_ALLOW_NEWER_SCHEMA=1 to open it anyway
```

`AO_ALLOW_NEWER_SCHEMA=1` turns the refusal off for both. It is a developer escape hatch, off by default; the daemon logs a warning on every start while it is set.

## Why

`goose.Up` returns nil when the database is ahead of the binary's embedded migrations, so an older build silently runs against a newer schema. That is the mechanism behind the schema-drift 500s in #4503 (#4335, #3476, #4415). Today only the updater's `allowDowngrade = false` protects users.

Refs #4503. This covers the refuse-newer part only (see Not covered).

## How

- **Rule.** Refuse when the highest applied migration in `goose_db_version` is above the highest migration this build embeds. "Applied" means the latest ledger row for that version says so, the same rule the repairs use.
- **What "above the head" means with timestamp IDs.** Migration IDs are now UTC creation timestamps (`YYYYMMDDHHMMSSsss`, `npm run migration:create`), so the rule compares creation times, not merge order:
  - A database that applied a migration created after this build's newest one is refused. That includes a dev build of an unmerged branch, not only a newer release. The refusal lifts by itself once the build contains any migration created later than that one.
  - A migration created before this build's newest one but merged after it is not detected, even when it ships only in a newer release. `WithAllowMissing` tolerates it as before.
- **Where.** The check runs inside the open call, before `migrate`. It only reads, and it runs before every repair, so a refused database is left exactly as found. A test pins this: with the check moved after `migrate`, the refused database gets its ledger rewritten (repair 179 to 190) and further migrations applied. Because the check lives inside the open call, the order with #6799 is data-dir lock, then schema check, then migrate, in both the daemon and `ao import`.
- **Why "above the head" and not "any version this build does not embed".** Real ledgers carry versions below the head that no embedded file claims: 22 (shipped in a nightly, then reverted), 45/46/50/51 (the foreign build of #3475, which recorded 40-51), 55-65 (pre-renumber chat branch, handled by `repairRenumberedChatMigrationHistory`), 182-184 (an unshipped cue branch, renumbered in f3f782f82f), 201/216 (provider-switching previews), and another branch's timestamp migration interleaved below the head (`TestMigrationsApplyOverAForeignInterleavedVersion`). Every existing renumbering repair maps old sequential numbers to canonical ones at or below the head, so none of them is affected. A set-difference rule would refuse all of these and strand installs that start today; `TestOpenIgnoresUnknownVersionsBelowTheEmbeddedHead` pins the sequential gaps plus one interleaved timestamp version.
- **Escape hatch: yes.** `~/.ao/dev/data` is the default data dir for every checkout's `npm run dev`, so developers on different branches share one database with different migration heads. Before this change that usually worked (at 0199, 125 of the 180 migrations contained no DROP or RENAME), so an older build tended to keep running against a schema that only gained objects. Without an override, the only way past the refusal is deleting dev data (or keeping a data dir per branch). The default stays refuse. `sqlite.Open(dir)` keeps its signature and always refuses; `sqlite.OpenWithSchemaPolicy(dir, allowNewerSchema)` is the one switch, and the daemon and `ao import` both pass `config.Config.AllowNewerSchema` to it. The variable is read in `config` like every other `AO_*` toggle (the storage package reads no environment). The daemon logs a warning on every start while it is set; `ao import`, a one-shot command, honours it without a warning line. I did not make dev builds bypass automatically: a dev daemon pointed at the real `~/.ao/data` is exactly where an older checkout must not silently open newer data.
- **`ao import`.** It opens `ao.db` itself, so it needs the same switch. Without it, import refused a newer database and its message told the user to set a variable that did nothing there. `TestImportCommand_NewerSchemaDatabase` covers both halves: refused by default, runs with the override.
- **Docs.** One row in the Daemon environment table (`frontend/src/docs/content/configuration/index.mdx`), and one line in `.agents/skills/ao-desktop-dev/SKILL.md` saying never to set it against real data, where it would let an older checkout open a database the installed app has already migrated past it.
- **Surfacing.** `Run` returns the error as `open store: ...`, `cli.Execute` prints it to stderr and exits 1; `ao import` returns the same error from `executeImport`. The desktop supervisor keeps the daemon's output and shows it under "Show details" in the "AO daemon failed to start" banner (`Daemon exited with code 1`). I read that path in `frontend/src/main.ts` and `DaemonFailureBanner.tsx`, and ran the real binary to capture the stderr line; I did not drive the Electron UI.
- **Rebased onto #6799** (data-dir lock). `executeImport` keeps main's `datadirlock.Acquire` block, including the `ErrUnsupported` fallback, and opens with `sqlite.OpenWithSchemaPolicy(cfg.DataDir, cfg.AllowNewerSchema)` after it. `config_test.go` keeps main's agent-browser tests next to this branch's toggle tests. `daemon.go` merged cleanly: `lockDataDir` still runs before `openStore`.
- **Timestamp IDs in the tests.** `sqlitetest.MustCreateNewerSchemaAt` recorded migration 99999, which is now below the head; it records `sqlitetest.NewerSchemaVersion` (a year-9999 timestamp ID) instead. The gap test walked every number up to the head, which never ends with a timestamp head; it now covers the sequential gaps plus `head-1`.

## Evidence

Measured in the shared perf lab on `7427cb8b4c`, the head of this branch before its first rebase, when migrations were still numbered `0NNN` (head 0199). The check, its message and the daemon's refusal path are unchanged since; only the ID format around them changed. The lab runs real `ao daemon` binaries under its sandbox on synthetic 864 KiB databases, merge-base against this branch, 5 runs per scenario with the order rotated (3 for the override). The "newer AO" is a throwaway local-only commit on top of this branch that adds a no-op migration 0200; its binary migrates a fresh data dir, and each build then starts on a copy.

| Scenario | Base `9ba118107b` | Branch `7427cb8b4c` |
|---|---|---|
| Start on a database a newer AO migrated (ledger max 0200) | **starts**: ready in 248 ms (216-2013); ledger unchanged; nothing about the schema in the log | **refuses**: exit 1 after 153 ms (79-209); one stderr line; ledger unchanged |
| Control: database at the build's own head (0199) | ready in 331 ms (256-506) | ready in 265 ms (154-1297) |
| Newer database with `AO_ALLOW_NEWER_SCHEMA=1` | no such switch | ready in 116 ms (86-119); warning logged in 3 of 3 runs |
| The check alone, in process (5,000 calls, 181-row ledger) | - | median 175 µs, p99 189 µs |

Median (min-max), spawn to `/readyz` 200, or spawn to exit for the refusing daemon. The machine was shared (load average 7 rising to 25), so the control rows only show that no startup cost is distinguishable from noise. Mac15,6 (M3 Pro), macOS 26.5.1, binaries built with go1.27.1. The harness, the raw JSON and a longer write-up are kept outside the repo. Not measured: the Electron banner (read in code, not driven), a real user database, and anything on the timestamp-ID head.

Process smoke on `461b5bd662` (pre-rebase, 0NNN IDs), real binary, isolated temp HOME and data dir, no sandbox: `ao import` into a fresh data dir exits 0. After the ledger gets a row 0200, `ao import` and `ao daemon` each exit 1 with the one-line message and an unchanged ledger, and `ao import` with `AO_ALLOW_NEWER_SCHEMA=1` exits 0 (0 imported, 1 already present).

## Testing

**The final head `2caaf7e2b3` is rebased onto main `9e347ec026` and was not re-run locally; CI covers it.** Everything below ran before the rebase, on the commits named, when migration IDs were still `0NNN`. `2caaf7e2b3` is new since then: it fixes the two test helpers that assumed sequential IDs (see How) and one comment. Commands ran from `backend/`.

- `dd5d10dc7e` (pre-rebase head): `gofmt -l .` clean; `go vet ./internal/cli ./internal/storage/sqlite` clean; `go test -race -count=1 -p 4 ./internal/cli -run Import` passes; `go test -count=1 -p 4 ./internal/storage/sqlite -run 'Newer|Schema'` passes. `TestImportCommand_NewerSchemaDatabase` also passes with `AO_ALLOW_NEWER_SCHEMA=1` exported in the environment; on `461b5bd662` it failed there with `err = <nil>`, because `setConfigEnv` does not clear the variable and the test's refusal half then ran with the override on.
- `461b5bd662`: `gofmt -l .` clean; `go build ./...` and `go vet ./...` clean; `golangci-lint run` (v2.13.2, as CI): 0 issues.
- `461b5bd662`: `go test -p 4 -count=1 ./...`: 199 packages pass, 14 have no tests, 2 fail. Both failures also occurred on unmodified main `5418c4631b` and depend on that machine: `opencodev2` `TestV2RejectsFailuresWithoutSideEffects` (OpenCode 1.19 installed) and `integration` `TestClaudeResumeHookConfirmsNativeIdentityForCurrentLaunch`.
- `461b5bd662`: `go test -race -p 4 -count=1 ./internal/config ./internal/daemon ./internal/cli` passes. The four `sqlite-race` shards, built with the exact commands from `.github/workflows/go.yml`, all pass.
- `461b5bd662`: docs. `npm run build` in `frontend/src/docs` passes and the built configuration page renders the new table row. No TypeScript changed.
- TDD. Before the first commit, the sqlite refusal tests failed on a compile-only stub (`Open` succeeded on a newer database), and the config and daemon tests did not compile. For the `ao import` fix, the new test failed on `8e117108a1` plus the test and its helper: with `AO_ALLOW_NEWER_SCHEMA=1` set, `ao import` still refused.
- `461b5bd662`, mutation checks in a temporary worktree: refusing the burned and foreign versions as well fails `TestOpenIgnoresUnknownVersionsBelowTheEmbeddedHead`; running the check after `migrate` fails `TestOpenRefusesNewerDatabaseBeforeRepairingLegacyHistory`.
- `2caaf7e2b3`: `gofmt -l` clean on the changed files. Nothing else run locally.

## Not covered

- **Builds that already shipped keep the old behaviour**, including the frozen npm CLI's daemon: they have no check, so they still open a newer database silently. Protection starts with the first release that contains this change.
- **The ledger stores migration numbers only.** A same-number, different-file collision between two builds still passes silently; this change detects only a database that is ahead of the binary.
- **Out-of-order merges.** A newer release whose only extra migrations were created before this build's newest one is not detected (see How). With timestamp IDs that is any long-lived branch merged after a newer migration.
- **Unmerged branch builds.** A dev build of a branch with a new migration, run against a shared data dir, makes every build without a later migration refuse that dir until `AO_ALLOW_NEWER_SCHEMA=1` is set or main gains a later migration. The message says "update AO", which does not help while that migration is unmerged.
- **The desktop experience.** The refusal reaches the user only as the generic "AO daemon failed to start / Daemon exited with code 1" banner, with the message under "Show details". Its Restart button cannot succeed against this error. A distinct exit code and banner copy are a follow-up (#6799 added exit code 75 for a locked data dir; this refusal still exits 1).
- **#6850** (pre-migration snapshot) adds `snapshotBeforeMigrate` on the same lines of `OpenWithSchemaPolicy`/`Open`. Whichever lands second resolves a one-line conflict; the refusal should stay before the snapshot so a refused database is not copied.
- The rest of #4503: stamping an app version in the database and a schema probe on `/readyz`.
- `OpenReadOnly`, used by the dev-import source, is not guarded. `ao import` prints no warning when the override is set.

title: feat(github): show the signed-in GitHub avatar in artifact history
body:
## What

Split out of #6753 at review. `GET /github/status` also returns `login`, the GitHub username AO is signed in as, and the artifact history menu shows that account's avatar on versions saved in the app. Stacked on #6753; retarget to `main` once it merges.

## Why separate

`/github/status` had no network dependency before. This adds an identity lookup, so it should be reviewable and revertable on its own.

## Backend

- `login` comes from the SCM provider (`AO_GITHUB_TOKEN`, then `gh auth token`). Empty when unknown.
- The lookup is capped at 2s, and a miss is remembered for 30s, so a machine without `gh` does not run `gh auth token` on every status request.

## Frontend

- A version saved in the app shows the GitHub avatar, titled with the username. Without a login it falls back to the plain user icon.

## How to test

1. Sign in with `gh auth login` (or set `AO_GITHUB_TOKEN`).
2. Open an artifact, save an edit, then open its History menu. Your save shows your GitHub avatar.
3. Sign out of `gh`; the row shows the plain user icon instead.

## Notes

- `githubStatusService.Login` has unit tests for the human-account check and the miss cache; the 2s timeout path is not tested.
